# Central vs. Peripheral Fatigue, and Low- vs. High-Frequency Fatigue

**What it is** — Fatigue during short-duration strength/power work is split into
**central fatigue** (reduced motivation, impaired spinal nerve transmission, reduced motor
neuron recruitment and firing rate — a CNS-level phenomenon) and **peripheral fatigue**
(failure somewhere in the excitation-contraction chain at the muscle cell itself: motor
end-plate, sarcolemma, T-tubules, sarcoplasmic reticulum, contractile proteins).
Peripheral fatigue further splits into **low-frequency fatigue** (impaired force at <20 Hz
stimulation, from depressed calcium release, with a prolonged recovery period "persisting
for as long as 48 hours," printed 15) and **high-frequency fatigue** (impaired force at
>50 Hz; the text gives no recovery-speed comparison between the two, printed 14-15).
Two distinct purposes are given for reduced central drive during fatigue, on different
pages: for short-term maximal contractions, the reduction in motor-neuron firing rate "may
be beneficial in avoiding electrical failure and facilitating maximal mechanical response"
(printed 15); separately, "muscle wisdom," the CNS's down-regulation of motor neuron
discharge rate during a sustained contraction, has a purpose "believed to ensure that
central neural drive to fatigued skeletal muscle matches that which is needed to generate
the required force," and "may be one mechanism that functions either to decrease or to
postpone central neural fatigue" (printed 16). Exercise-induced ammonia accumulation is
cited as a possible contributor to central fatigue at high intensities/durations. Intensive
CNS activation (max weights, max power, plyometrics) is stated to need at least 48 hours of
recovery if no restorative methods are used. (PDF pp. 24-27, printed pp. 13-16.)

**Why it works** — Fatigue is not a single process with one cause; the central/peripheral
split and the frequency-dependent split reflect genuinely different physiological
bottlenecks (nervous drive vs. contractile-machinery failure vs. calcium-handling
kinetics), which is why they have different time courses and respond to different
recovery strategies.

**When to apply** — The authors state intensive CNS activation (max weights, max power,
plyometrics) needs at least 48 hours of recovery if no restorative methods are used (PDF p.
26, printed p. 15). **Inference:** this supports spacing high-CNS-cost sessions (max
strength, high-velocity work) at least two days apart within a microcycle, and treating
"still feels flat two days after a max-effort day" as plausible central fatigue rather than
assuming poor effort or motivation; this specific practical framing is not stated in the
text.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a mechanistic taxonomy from exercise
physiology, not a monitoring protocol. **Eric's baseline:** modified reactive strength
index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing is the department's chosen daily readiness marker
(`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
`2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`); **Inference:** mRSI is a downstream readiness proxy,
not a direct central/peripheral fatigue assay, so a flat CMJ day should not be
over-attributed to a specific named mechanism (e.g., "low-frequency fatigue") without EMG
or stimulation data — neither source states this equivalence, and this caution is this
entry's own judgment.

**Example** — Inference: a depressed CMJ the day after max squats more likely reflects
residual fatigue than lost strength; retest at 48 hours rather than reacting to a single
depressed value.

**Related** — [[framework--factors-limiting-strength-production]].

# Estimating Strength Deficit by Comparing a Static-Start Jump to a Dip/Countermovement Jump

**What it is** — Strength deficit is defined as the gap between an athlete's maximum
voluntary strength in a given action and their absolute strength (Fmm), the involuntary
ceiling for that same action (see [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]]), "the
difference between maximum strength (voluntary effort) produced in a given action and
absolute strength (involuntary effort) of which the athlete is capable in that same
action" (printed 9). True Fmm requires electrical stimulation, which is impractical and
risky to test directly. As a field proxy, the text proposes comparing a vertical jump from
a static, knees-flexed start (no countermovement) against a vertical jump preceded by a
sudden dip (printed 9).

The book gives two different, conflicting rules for what a small versus large gap means,
and this entry previously took only one side. The jump paragraph itself states: "If there
is a small difference between the two jumps, this suggests that training focuses more on
nervous stimulation via the use of 'shock' and ballistic methods such as plyometrics. If
the deficit is large, then strength and hypertrophy training with 5RM to 8RM ... loads
using methods such as CAT (Compensatory Activation Training) is more suitable" (printed
9-10). The very next paragraph states the opposite pairing as a general rule: "In general,
if the strength deficit is large for a given muscle group, an increase in speed-strength
may be produced by maximal or near-maximal neuromuscular stimulation (e.g. via
weightlifting or plyometric methods). If the strength deficit is small, hypertrophy must be
induced by submaximal loading methods" (printed 10). These two statements directly
conflict on the jump test's own page: a small jump-test gap means shock/ballistic work by
the first statement and hypertrophy-then-heavy-loads by the second; a large gap means
5-8RM CAT strength/hypertrophy work by the first statement and weightlifting/plyometric
work by the second. No direction can be safely taken from this source alone. (PDF pp.
20-21, printed pp. 9-10; the explosive-strength-deficit formalism, Fmax vs. Fmm, is
credited to Zatsiorsky, 1995, discussed further via the force-time curve in Ch3.)

The vault's summary of Kozinc et al. (2022) similarly concludes that a larger CMJ-SJ
difference "is not necessarily better" and "does not validate a diagnostic cutoff or a
training algorithm" (`kozinc-2022-the-difference-between-squat-jump-and-countermovement-jump-in-770-male-and-female-particip`),
which independently argues against using either of this book's two directions as a
programming rule.

**Why it works** — Inference: a countermovement recruits the stretch-shortening cycle and
a degree of involuntary reflex potentiation that a static start cannot access, which is
presumably why the book treats the gap as informative at all; but because the book gives
opposite readings of what a large or small gap implies, no mechanism can be assigned with
confidence to either direction.

**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** the standard CMJ family run on ForceDecks
includes the squat jump (quarter-squat start, static, 3s hold) and the countermovement
jump (x3), among other variants (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular
monitoring," citing `revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`); mRSI from daily CMJ testing is
the department's chosen daily readiness marker (same section, citing
`2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`). Inference: SJ-vs-CMJ comparison on ForceDecks is a
modern, instrumented analogue of this book's proposed proxy, but given the book's internal
conflict and Kozinc et al. (2022)'s finding that the difference does not validate a
training algorithm, this entry gives no basis for deriving a training-emphasis rule from
that comparison.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not use this framework to set training emphasis from an
SJ/CMJ-style gap in either direction; the book contradicts itself on which direction is
which (printed 9-10), and the modern evidence on this specific test (Kozinc et al. 2022)
does not support a diagnostic cutoff or algorithm built on it. Use RSI, mRSI, or other
modern jump-testing metrics on their own validated basis instead of this 1990s-era
heuristic.

**Example** — Inference: no training-emphasis direction can be taken from this source; see
Kozinc et al. (2022) for the modern evidence on SJ-CMJ differences.

**Related** — [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]],
[[research-papers/kozinc-2022-the-difference-between-squat-jump-and-countermovement-jump-in-770-male-and-female-particip]].

# The Same Force (F = ma) Produced Different Ways Trains Differently

**What it is** — Newton's second law (F = ma) means the same force can be produced with a
large mass and small acceleration (powerlifting-style, heavy load), a small mass and large
acceleration (many track and field actions), a moderate mass and moderate acceleration
(bodybuilding-style hypertrophy training, roughly 8-12 reps), or near-zero acceleration
under isometric/isokinetic conditions. Despite equal force output, these methods are
argued and shown in practice not to produce the same training effect, because different
neural, muscular, and metabolic processes are engaged in each case. (PDF pp. 32-33,
printed pp. 21-22.)

**Why it works** — The text bases the "do not produce the same results" claim on "practical
experience from three different competitive aspects of strength training" (powerlifting,
weightlifting, bodybuilding; printed 22), not on a stated mechanism. Inference: force alone
does not specify the movement's velocity, duration, muscle action type, or motor unit
recruitment/firing pattern, all of which independently affect the training stimulus; two
efforts that reach the same peak force via different mass-acceleration combinations are
mechanically equal on that one variable but different on several others that matter
physiologically.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a reasoning check against choosing exercises
solely by "how much force does this produce," when the intended adaptation (max strength
vs. explosive power vs. hypertrophy vs. isometric endurance) requires matching the
mass-acceleration profile, not just the force magnitude, to the target quality. This
generalized application is this entry's own extension of the four loading-option
comparison (PDF pp. 32-33, printed pp. 21-22).

**When NOT to apply** — The authors state isokinetic training (option d, F = k.R)
correlates poorly with actual sporting performance despite producing meaningful
non-specific strength gains in a lab setting (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22, citing Rosentzweig
& Hinson 1972, Ostemig 1986). **Inference:** don't treat isokinetic results as a proxy for
how an athlete will perform in ballistic, free-loading sport actions; this specific
caution is this entry's own restatement of that finding's practical implication.
Inference: for hypertrophy specifically, load magnitude matters less than effort: similar
hypertrophy is reported across a wide load range when sets are taken to failure (Schoenfeld
et al. 2017, JSCR), so the "do not produce the same results" claim is more load-outcome-
specific than the text's general statement suggests.

**Example** — **Inference:** A powerlifting-style heavy squat and an Olympic-style ballistic
clean pull can both produce a similar peak force at the bar, but the clean pull's high
acceleration under a lighter relative load trains rate of force development and ballistic
coordination that the heavy, slow squat does not, and vice versa for maximal-tension
adaptation.

**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]].

# Seven Factors That Limit Strength Production

**What it is** — Strength output in the short and long term is limited by seven
interacting factors: **trainability** (genetic ceiling for hypertrophy, fibre-type
distribution, leverage, and pre-training status); **neuromuscular efficiency** (skill in
recruiting the right muscles accurately and powerfully); **biomechanical efficiency**
(leverage and relative muscle-group strength, trainable unlike raw genetic trainability);

# Biochemical Adaptations Occur in a Fixed Order, and Reverse in the Opposite Order When Training Stops

**What it is** — Citing Platonov (1988), the authors state biochemical adaptation to
training follows a definite three-stage sequence, not a simultaneous shift: first,
oxidative ATP resynthesis potential and glycogen level increase; next, structural muscle
protein (myosin) and the intensity of non-oxidative ATP resynthesis (glycolysis) increase;
only after that does creatine phosphate (CP) level rise. During overtraining specifically,
these adaptations are lost "in an order that is the reverse of the order seen during
training." The longer the training period, the more thorough the adaptation and the longer
those biochemical changes persist after training stops (especially glycogen and CP levels).
This gain/loss asymmetry across different systems is termed heterochronic (different
tissues and processes change on different timelines). Overtraining specifically also shows
a distinct pattern: reduced glycogenolytic activity, decreased ascorbic acid/glutathione/
glycogen, blood plasma dysproteinaemia, and reduced sympathico-adrenal function tied to
disrupted acid-base balance. (PDF pp. 96-97, printed pp. 85-86.)

**Why it works** — Inference: different adaptations (enzymatic/oxidative capacity,
structural protein synthesis, phosphagen system capacity) depend on different cellular
mechanisms with different synthesis and degradation rates, so a uniform "the body adapts,
then de-adapts" model misses that some qualities are gained early and lost late, while
others are gained late and lost early. The author gives no such mechanism directly; this is
this entry's own reading of the stated sequence.

**When to apply** — **Eric's baseline:** the department's own conditioning material states
that traits easiest to build (aerobic) are lost fastest under detraining, while traits
hardest to build (alactic/speed) are lost slowest, and uses this ordering to sequence how
often each quality needs re-exposure (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy
systems," citing `class-4-2026.md p.47`). **Inference:** this converges directionally with
Platonov's heterochronic principle (different systems have different adaptation/de-
adaptation timelines) but the two are not a stated one-to-one match — the baseline's
build-easy/lose-fast claim is about energy-system categories (aerobic vs. alactic), while
Platonov's sequence is about biochemical sub-processes within training generally (oxidative
capacity, structural protein, glycolysis, CP). Treat them as parallel instances of the same
underlying heterochronicity concept, not as the same specific claim restated.

**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** the specific ordering (oxidative/glycogen, then
structural protein/glycolysis, then CP) is cited to one secondary source (Platonov, 1988)
without the underlying primary data described in this text; do not treat this exact
three-stage sequence as a settled, universally-timed protocol for monitoring detraining. Use
it as a general principle (adaptation and loss are not uniform across systems) rather than
a specific testing checklist. The source states the reverse-order loss for overtraining,
not for simple layoffs; the entry's own extension to detraining/layoffs beyond what the
text states is this entry's inference, not the authors' claim.

**Example** — Inference: by the stated reverse order, CP-related qualities (gained last)
would be lost first, and oxidative and glycogen qualities lost last. The source states this
reverse order for overtraining, not for a training layoff; it separately notes that longer
training makes the accompanying biochemical changes persist longer after cessation
(printed 86), which is the closest the text comes to describing simple detraining.

joint is well documented; return to top performance depends on the athlete's own
perception that rehab is complete, not just medical clearance); and **fatigue** (central
vs. peripheral, discussed further in
[[framework--central-vs-peripheral-fatigue-mechanisms]]). (PDF pp. 23-24, printed pp.
12-13.)

volume, and technique, but this list makes explicit that psychological state, injury
history, and perceived pain/fear operate as real physiological limiters on force output.

which produces muscle weakness when a joint is damaged" (Stokes & Young, 1984; printed 14).

measurable neuromuscular effect, not a motivation problem.

athlete perceives rehabilitation to be complete" and the fear of pain or re-injury being

`baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.6`); that same baseline section is flagged as

# Restrictive, Repetitive Patterns May Overspecialize the Nervous System

**What it is** — Drawing on neuroplasticity research (Rosenzweig, Diamond, Greenough,
cortical reorganization in amputees and stroke patients), the text argues the nervous
system rewires quickly (within minutes, not years) around whatever movement pattern is
repeated, and lists practical inferences: avoid machines that restrict joint movement to
one plane/pattern (they can reprogram the brain toward that restricted pattern and reduce
sport-specific capability); avoid over-reliance on ergogenic devices (lifting belts, wrist
wraps, shoe wedges) that can make efficient unassisted movement harder later; favor
planned variation of means, methods, and exercises over fixed repetition of the same
weights or machines; respect individual movement style rather than forcing one stereotyped
technique on every athlete. (PDF pp. 19-20, printed pp. 8-9.)

**Why it works** — Inference: the underlying neuroscience (adult cortical plasticity, rapid
synaptic change, constraint-induced reorganization in rehab patients) is well established.
The extension to healthy-athlete strength training — that machine use or ergogenic aids
will measurably "reprogram" sport-specific neural patterns — is the text's own inference,
not a finding directly tested in athletes in this section.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** this can be used as a rationale for favoring
free-weight, multi-planar, compound movement over single-joint machine work when the goal
is direct transfer to a sport skill, and for planning intentional exercise variation
across a training block rather than running the same fixed machine circuit indefinitely.
**Eric's baseline:** the department teaches "knowledge from experience" as an operating
value: keep things simple, teach basic movement skills and basic lifts before anything
advanced, and require bodyweight competency before loaded work
(`method-baseline.md`, "Philosophy and decision principles," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.4-5`, `week1-lecture.md p.12`). **Inference:**
that basic-movement-first philosophy is broadly consistent with this heuristic's caution
about restrictive machine patterns, though the baseline material does not itself cite a
neuroplasticity mechanism or single out machines specifically.

**When NOT to apply** — This entry is rated `contested` where it implies routine machine
use or belts during max lifts causes lasting neural harm to sport skill; the text (PDF pp.
19-20, printed pp. 8-9) gives no dose-response evidence for that extension. The named
counterpoint: injury-prevention evidence for lifting belts is itself weak (e.g. NIOSH,
1994, found insufficient evidence that belts reduce back-injury risk), and studies
comparing machine and free-weight training have found similar strength gains between the
two, which cuts against treating machines as uniquely "restrictive" in outcome terms.
**Inference:** this passage gives no evidence on belts either way; do not use this
heuristic, in either direction, to make a safety claim about belts for heavy compound
lifts.

**Example** — **Inference:** Programming a hip-thrust machine as the sole posterior-chain exercise for a
sprinter, with no free-weight hip hinge or sprint-pattern work anywhere in the week, is the
scenario this heuristic warns against; it does not warn against occasional supported
machine use as part of a varied program.

**Related** — [[framework--functional-vs-structural-resistance-training]].

-# "Adaptive Reconstruction" vs. "Supercompensation": Verkhoshansky/Siff's Sharper Critique
-**What it is** — The authors argue "adaptive reconstruction" is a more accurate term than
-"supercompensation" for the body's response to training load. One reason is stated
-directly alongside the term: enhanced performance "is not simply the result of increased
-stores of bioenergetic substances, but also of structural changes in muscle and other
-tissues, as well as enhanced efficiency and rates of bioenergetic and neuromuscular
-processing" (printed 84). A second reason comes not from that passage but from the
-separate single-factor-model critique in 1.16.3: ATP "has never been shown to deplete
-significantly, even after very strenuous exercise," and "no supercompensation has yet been
-observed to occur among any of the other biochemicals" besides glycogen; each substance
-returns to its initial level on its own timeline, so "the timing of subsequent loads to
-stimulate the appropriate type of supercompensation remains indeterminate" (printed 87-88).
-The book gives two different definitions of "Current Adaptation Reserves" (CAR) for
-opposite ends of the same distinction: printed 83 states "In Russian texts, the former
-[i.e. the readily-available, superficial] energy source is referred to as the Current
-Adaptation Reserves (CAR)," while the Fig 1.39 caption on printed 84 states "The Deep
-Adaptation Energy is often referred to as the Current Adaptation Reserves (CAR) by Russian
-authors." Both are recorded here rather than harmonized.
-The book also conflicts with itself on supercompensation: printed 85 (citing Platonov,
-1988) states "supercompensation of some of the energy sources takes place," while printed
-88 states "No supercompensation has yet been observed to occur among any of the other
-biochemicals." (PDF pp. 94-99, printed pp. 83-88.)
-**Why it works** — Inference: if supercompensation literally meant every adaptation-relevant
-substance or structure overshoots baseline on a predictable clock, timing the next training
-stimulus to "catch the peak" would be a precise science; the book's own admission that this
-overshoot pattern is not established for biochemicals besides glycogen undercuts that
-precision and supports treating "the next stimulus should land on a rebound" as a general
-heuristic, not a substance-by-substance timing rule.
-**When to apply** — This library already carries the supercompensation model in
-[[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle]], which itself notes
-"contemporary sport science largely prefers the fitness-fatigue (two-factor) model over
-literal supercompensation" and recommends treating supercompensation "as a useful mental
-model, not a measured prescription." **Inference:** this entry adds the specific mechanism
-for that caution (structural/efficiency changes beyond energy stores, and the
-glycogen-only overshoot finding) and the CAR terminology, which the Bompa entry does not
-include; use both together rather than duplicating either.
-**When NOT to apply** — This entry is rated `contested` because it is itself a critique of
-a still widely-taught model (supercompensation), argued from a mix of established fact
-(structural adaptation beyond energy stores) and an absence-of-evidence claim (no
-overshoot observed for other biochemicals) that could be revised by newer measurement
-techniques. **Inference:** don't treat "adaptive reconstruction" as a rejection of
-periodization practice built on supercompensation timing; the text itself notes
-supercompensation theory, despite its shortcomings, had a profound and still-useful impact
-on periodization design.
-**Example** — **Inference:** glycogen loading before an endurance event is a legitimate
-application of true supercompensation; assuming a similarly precise "peak window" exists
-for, say, connective tissue remodeling or neuromuscular efficiency gains is not supported
-by the same evidence.
-**Related** — [[periodization--bompa/principle--supercompensation-cycle]] (reciprocal link
-recommended there: note that Supertraining Ch1.16 sharpens the "useful mental model, not a
-measured prescription" caution with the specific glycogen-only-overshoot finding and the
-CAR/adaptive-reconstruction terminology).

-# The Bilateral Deficit: Two Limbs Together Produce Less Force Than the Sum of Each Alone
-**What it is** — Force produced during a bilateral (two-limb, e.g. barbell) contraction is
-usually less than the sum of the forces each limb produces individually (e.g. dumbbells),
-a phenomenon called the bilateral deficit, accompanied by reduced integrated EMG
-suggesting the prime movers are less activated bilaterally (Coyle et al. 1981;
-Vandervoort et al. 1984). The deficit is reported as insignificant in athletes who always
-use their limbs simultaneously in their sport (e.g. weightlifters), and the text
-recommends athletes whose sport involves bilateral action of the same muscle groups train
-bilaterally to minimize the deficit (Secher, 1975). (PDF p. 39, printed p. 28.)
-**Why it works** — The reduced integrated EMG "suggest[s] that the prime movers were less
-activated" during bilateral effort (printed 28). Inference: the absence of a deficit in
-weightlifters, who train the bilateral pattern extensively, suggests it is trainable.
-**When to apply** — **Inference:** when deciding whether to prioritize bilateral (back
-squat, bench, clean) or unilateral (split squat, single-leg press, lunge) exercise
-variants, match the training mode to how the sport actually loads the limbs. For sports
-with genuinely unilateral force production (sprinting, most cutting and
-change-of-direction actions), this text's finding argues for meaningful unilateral training
-exposure, not exclusively bilateral lifts, since bilateral-only training may under-develop
-the single-limb activation football and track actions require. This football-specific
-application is this entry's own extension, not stated in the text.
-**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** do not use this to argue against bilateral lifts
-altogether; compound bilateral lifts remain valuable for maximal strength and are
-appropriate where the sport itself uses bilateral effort (e.g. some blocking or lifting
-actions). The text gives no specific deficit magnitude for team-sport athletes in
-this section (PDF p. 39, printed p. 28); **Inference:** the deficit's size and
-trainability likely vary by athlete and lift, which is this entry's own caution.
-**Example** — Inference: single-leg strength work trains the unilateral expression that
-sprint and cutting actions use; bilateral 1RM alone may not show it.
-**Related** — [[principle--specificity-of-training-ten-dimensions]],
-[[fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/claim--unilateral-isometric-exposes-hidden-asymmetry]].

-# Collagenous Tissue's Four-Region Loading Curve, and Why Loading Rate Changes What Fails First
-**What it is** — Collagenous tissue (e.g. the ACL, studied by Frankel & Nordin 1980)
-loaded to failure shows four regions: Region I, the "toe region," where the crimped
-tissue straightens with little force and mild stretching here produces no long-term
-flexibility change; Region II, a near-linear region where fibres are fully uncrimped and
-parallel; Region III, where sequential microfailure of overstretched fibres begins; Region
-IV, complete failure. Loading rate changes the outcome: increasing loading rate roughly
-fourfold raised knee ligament failure load by almost 50% (Kennedy et al., 1976), and which
-structure fails first flips with rate — at slow loading rates the ligament's bony
-insertion is the weakest link, while at fast loading rates the ligament itself is the
-weakest link (bone's strength rises faster with rate than the ligament's). Healthy tendon's
-tensile strength can be more than twice that of its associated muscle, which is why
-ruptures are more common in muscle than tendon. (PDF pp. 54-56, printed pp. 43-45.)
-**Why it works** — Collagen is viscoelastic: it behaves more elastically under rapid
-loading and more plastically (creeping, deforming) under slow, sustained loading, so both
-the loading speed and the tissue's own rate-dependent stiffness change determine where in
-the body an excessive load actually causes failure.
-**When to apply** — **Inference:** relevant background for understanding why static
-stretching held gently (Region I) does not meaningfully change tissue length or
-flexibility over time, and why ballistic or rapid loading, once past Region II, carries
-real microfailure risk; also relevant context for why the pattern of injury (bone
-avulsion vs. mid-ligament tear vs. muscle strain) can differ by the speed of the loading
-event, which matters for how Athletic Medicine and Applied Performance jointly interpret
-an injury mechanism.
-**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is basic tissue mechanics from cited
-1970s-1980s cadaveric/animal ligament research, not a live-tissue, in-vivo human athlete
-dataset; do not use the specific numbers (50% failure-load increase, the fourfold rate
-figure) as applicable outside the original knee-ligament loading-rate study (Kennedy 1976,
-printed 44); only the strain curve (Fig 1.21) is specifically ACL.
-This is background science, not a clinical decision rule, and should not substitute for
-Athletic Medicine's own injury assessment framework.
-**Example** — **Inference:** a sudden high-rate valgus load to the knee is more likely to
-produce mid-ligament ACL failure, while a slower, sustained load is more likely to fail at
-the bony insertion first; this pattern helps explain, but does not replace, imaging and
-clinical exam in determining actual injury location.
-**Related** — [[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]],
-[[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]].

-# Continuous Circuit Training Does Not Simultaneously Build Strength and Endurance; Interval Circuit Training Is a Better Fit
-**What it is** — Research does not support the claim (made by some instructors and machine
-manufacturers) that continuous circuit training (CCT) simultaneously develops
-cardiovascular endurance and strength. Interval circuit training (ICT: high-intensity
-loading with regular rest intervals) is described as more suitable for developing strength
-and strength-endurance together. Supporting evidence cited: prolonged low-intensity
-endurance training performed alongside strength training in the same phase seriously
-compromises strength/power development, partly because fast-twitch fibres can start
-behaving like slow-twitch fibres under prolonged low-intensity load; muscle biopsy studies
-of distance runners' gastrocnemius after a marathon show necrosis and inflammation
-detectable at least 7 days later, an abnormality not seen in comparable biopsies from
-weightlifters, sprinters, or rowers after strenuous sessions. (PDF p. 70, printed p. 59.)
-**Why it works** — The author gives one mechanism: fast-twitch fibres can start behaving
-like slow-twitch fibres under prolonged low-intensity work (printed 59). Inference:
-continuous, moderate-intensity circuit work biases fibre behavior toward slow-twitch
-characteristics, a different and partly conflicting neuromuscular target from the
-high-force, high-velocity, largely fast-twitch demands of strength and power work; ICT's
-rest intervals let each work bout stay in a higher-intensity, more strength/power-specific
-zone instead of drifting toward an endurance stimulus.
-**When to apply** — **Inference:** relevant when designing off-season/GPP programming
-that needs to develop both conditioning and strength: the text's recommendation is to
-prescribe cardiovascular training separately, in limited amounts, early in the off-season,
-with higher-intensity resistance training emphasized later, and to use interval-style
-(work/rest) circuits rather than continuous circuits when the goal includes
-strength-endurance. **Eric's baseline:** this converges with the department's own
-conditioning priority stack for football (alactic and aerobic capacity/power first, with
-glycolytic conditioning absorbed incidentally rather than programmed as a primary target;
-`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy systems," citing `class-4-2026.md pp.34,
-39`), though the baseline material does not itself cite this fibre-type mechanism.
-**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is evidence against combining continuous,
-prolonged low-intensity work with concurrent strength training in the same block, not an
-argument against all conditioning; short, high-intensity interval conditioning is treated
-as more compatible with strength/power goals. The gastrocnemius necrosis finding is
-specific to marathon-distance running, not necessarily to all forms of aerobic
-conditioning used in team-sport contexts. The authors also state that ICT's own
-sub-maximal nature "does not enhance strength and power sufficiently to meet the specific
-needs of strength and speed sports, except possibly during the early off-season" (PDF p.
-91, printed p. 80); ICT is a better fit than CCT for concurrent goals, not a substitute for
-dedicated strength/power training.
-**Example** — **Inference:** programming continuous, moderate-pace circuit stations as a
-"two birds, one stone" strength-and-conditioning solution is not well supported by this
-evidence; separating a short conditioning block from resistance training, or using
-interval-format circuits with real rest between high-intensity efforts, is the better-
-supported approach.
-**Related** — [[claim--fiber-recruitment-not-simply-graded-by-force]].

-# Muscle Adapts in Days; Tendon, Ligament, and Bone Take Weeks to Months
-**What it is** — Muscle tissue adapts to increased loading within several days, whereas
-connective tissues (tendon, ligament, joint capsule) and tissue systems with a high
-connective-tissue content (bone, cartilage) only show significant adaptation and
-hypertrophy after several weeks to months of progressive loading (McDonagh & Davies,
-1984). The authors state training prescription must account for the different
-adaptation rates of all involved systems and avoid overtraining whichever system adapts
-slowest; they recommend gradual load increases and avoiding impulsive/explosive methods
-particularly during General Physical Preparation (GPP) and for relative novices to
-strength training. (PDF p. 46, printed p. 35.)
-**Why it works** — The author gives no mechanism beyond the differing rates. Inference:
-collagen turnover and remodeling are slower than muscle protein synthesis and neural
-adaptation, so a program that progresses load at the muscle's adaptation rate can outpace
-what tendon, ligament, and bone can structurally tolerate.
-**When to apply** — **Inference:** directly supports conservative, gradual load
-progression in GPP/early training blocks and for novice athletes specifically, and argues
-against introducing high-impulse plyometric or explosive work before a base period of
-progressive loading has given connective tissue time to adapt. This is a mechanistic
-rationale for why "the athlete feels ready for more" (muscle-level readiness) is not
-sufficient justification for a rapid load jump (tendon/bone-level readiness lags behind).
-**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this passage gives no specific timeline (only
-"several days" vs. "several weeks or months") and no athlete-population-specific data; do
-not treat it as a precise dosing table. **Inference:** this is a general injury-risk
-mechanism, not a substitute for clinical input from Athletic Medicine on a specific
-athlete's tissue status or injury history.
-**Example** — **Inference:** a novice athlete whose squat strength (muscle-level) is
-progressing quickly should still have their loading ramp paced by a longer timeline
-(weeks to months) appropriate to tendon and bone adaptation, not by how fast their 1RM is
-climbing.
-**Related** — [[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]].

+# Muscle Adapts in Days; Tendon, Ligament, and Bone Take Weeks to Months
+**What it is:** Muscle tissue adapts to increased loading within several days, whereas
+connective tissues (tendon, ligament, joint capsule) and tissue systems with a high
+connective-tissue content (bone, cartilage) only show significant adaptation and
+hypertrophy after several weeks to months of progressive loading (McDonagh & Davies,
+1984). The authors state training prescription must account for the different
+adaptation rates of all involved systems and avoid overtraining whichever system adapts
+slowest; they recommend gradual load increases and avoiding impulsive/explosive methods
+particularly during General Physical Preparation (GPP) and for relative novices to
+strength training. (PDF p. 46, printed p. 35.)
+**Why it works:** The author gives no mechanism beyond the differing rates. Inference:
+collagen turnover and remodeling are slower than muscle protein synthesis and neural
+adaptation, so a program that progresses load at the muscle's adaptation rate can outpace
+what tendon, ligament, and bone can structurally tolerate.
+**When to apply:** **Inference:** directly supports conservative, gradual load
+progression in GPP/early training blocks and for novice athletes specifically, and argues
+against introducing high-impulse plyometric or explosive work before a base period of
+progressive loading has given connective tissue time to adapt. This is a mechanistic
+rationale for why "the athlete feels ready for more" (muscle-level readiness) is not
+sufficient justification for a rapid load jump (tendon/bone-level readiness lags behind).
+**When NOT to apply:** **Inference:** this passage gives no specific timeline (only
+"several days" vs. "several weeks or months") and no athlete-population-specific data; do
+not treat it as a precise dosing table. **Inference:** this is a general injury-risk
+mechanism, not a substitute for clinical input from Athletic Medicine on a specific
+athlete's tissue status or injury history.
+**Example:** **Inference:** a novice athlete whose squat strength (muscle-level) is
+progressing quickly should still have their loading ramp paced by a longer timeline
+(weeks to months) appropriate to tendon and bone adaptation, not by how fast their 1RM is
+climbing.
+**Related:** [[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]].

14	# The Same Force (F = ma) Produced Different Ways Trains Differently
15	
16	**What it is:** Newton's second law (F = ma) means the same force can be produced with a
17	large mass and small acceleration (powerlifting-style, heavy load), a small mass and large
18	acceleration (many track and field actions), a moderate mass and moderate acceleration
19	(bodybuilding-style hypertrophy training, roughly 8-12 reps), or near-zero acceleration
20	under isometric/isokinetic conditions. Despite equal force output, these methods are
21	argued and shown in practice not to produce the same training effect, because different
22	neural, muscular, and metabolic processes are engaged in each case. (PDF pp. 32-33,
23	printed pp. 21-22.)
24	
25	**Why it works:** The text bases the "do not produce the same results" claim on "practical
26	experience from three different competitive aspects of strength training" (powerlifting,
27	weightlifting, bodybuilding; printed 22), not on a stated mechanism. Inference: force alone
28	does not specify the movement's velocity, duration, muscle action type, or motor unit
29	recruitment/firing pattern, all of which independently affect the training stimulus; two
30	efforts that reach the same peak force via different mass-acceleration combinations are
31	mechanically equal on that one variable but different on several others that matter
32	physiologically.
33	
34	**When to apply:** **Inference:** usable as a reasoning check against choosing exercises
35	solely by "how much force does this produce," when the intended adaptation (max strength
36	vs. explosive power vs. hypertrophy vs. isometric endurance) requires matching the
37	mass-acceleration profile, not just the force magnitude, to the target quality. This
38	generalized application is this entry's own extension of the four loading-option
39	comparison (PDF pp. 32-33, printed pp. 21-22).
40	
41	**When NOT to apply:** The authors state isokinetic training (option d, F = k.R)
42	correlates poorly with actual sporting performance despite producing meaningful
43	non-specific strength gains in a lab setting (PDF p. 33, printed p. 22, citing Rosentzweig
44	& Hinson 1972, Osternig 1986). **Inference:** don't treat isokinetic results as a proxy for
45	how an athlete will perform in ballistic, free-loading sport actions; this specific
46	caution is this entry's own restatement of that finding's practical implication.
47	Inference: for hypertrophy specifically, load magnitude matters less than effort: similar
48	hypertrophy is reported across a wide load range when sets are taken to failure (Schoenfeld
49	et al. 2017, JSCR), so the "do not produce the same results" claim is more load-outcome-
50	specific than the text's general statement suggests.
51	
52	**Example:** **Inference:** A powerlifting-style heavy squat and an Olympic-style ballistic
53	clean pull can both produce a similar peak force at the bar, but the clean pull's high
54	acceleration under a lighter relative load trains rate of force development and ballistic
55	coordination that the heavy, slow squat does not, and vice versa for maximal-tension
56	adaptation.
57	
58	**Related:** [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]].

14	# Central vs. Peripheral Fatigue, and Low- vs. High-Frequency Fatigue
15	
16	**What it is:** Fatigue during short-duration strength/power work is split into
17	**central fatigue** (reduced motivation, impaired spinal nerve transmission, reduced motor
18	neuron recruitment and firing rate — a CNS-level phenomenon) and **peripheral fatigue**
19	(failure somewhere in the excitation-contraction chain at the muscle cell itself: motor
20	end-plate, sarcolemma, T-tubules, sarcoplasmic reticulum, contractile proteins).
21	Peripheral fatigue further splits into **low-frequency fatigue** (impaired force at <20 Hz
22	stimulation, from depressed calcium release, with a prolonged recovery period "persisting
23	for as long as 48 hours," printed 15) and **high-frequency fatigue** (impaired force at
24	>50 Hz; the text gives no recovery-speed comparison between the two, printed 14-15).
...
29	discharge rate during a sustained contraction, has a purpose "believed to ensure that
30	central neural drive to fatigued skeletal muscle matches that which is needed to generate
31	the required force," and "may be one mechanism that functions either to decrease or to
32	postpone central neural fatigue" (printed 16). Exercise-induced ammonia accumulation is
33	cited as a possible contributor to central fatigue at high intensities/durations. Intensive
34	CNS activation (max weights, max power, plyometrics) is stated to need at least 48 hours of
35	recovery if no restorative methods are used. (PDF pp. 24-27, printed pp. 13-16.)
36	
37	**Why it works:** Inference: fatigue is not a single process with one cause; the
38	central/peripheral split and the frequency-dependent split reflect genuinely different
39	physiological bottlenecks (nervous drive vs. contractile-machinery failure vs.
40	calcium-handling kinetics), which is why they have different time courses.
41	
42	**When to apply:** The authors state intensive CNS activation (max weights, max power,
43	plyometrics) needs at least 48 hours of recovery if no restorative methods are used (PDF p.
44	26, printed p. 15). **Inference:** this supports spacing high-CNS-cost sessions (max
45	strength, high-velocity work) at least two days apart within a microcycle, and treating
46	"still feels flat two days after a max-effort day" as plausible central fatigue rather than
47	assuming poor effort or motivation; this specific practical framing is not stated in the
48	text.
49	
50	**When NOT to apply:** **Inference:** this is a mechanistic taxonomy from exercise
51	physiology, not a monitoring protocol. **Eric's baseline:** modified reactive strength
52	index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing is the department's chosen daily readiness marker
53	(`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
54	`2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`); **Inference:** mRSI is a downstream readiness proxy,
55	not a direct central/peripheral fatigue assay, so a flat CMJ day should not be
56	over-attributed to a specific named mechanism (e.g., "low-frequency fatigue") without EMG
57	or stimulation data — neither source states this equivalence, and this caution is this
58	entry's own judgment.
59	
60	**Example:** Inference: a depressed CMJ the day after max squats more likely reflects
61	residual fatigue than lost strength; retest at 48 hours rather than reacting to a single
62	depressed value.

14	# Strength Training Adapts Along (at Least) Ten Independent, Narrow Dimensions
15	
16	**What it is:** Strength gains transfer narrowly, not generally, across at least ten
17	independent dimensions: type of muscle contraction, movement pattern, region/range of
18	movement, velocity of movement, force of contraction, muscle fibre recruitment,
19	metabolism, biochemical adaptation, flexibility, and fatigue. Training that improves one
20	dimension often produces little or no improvement on the others, even when the same
21	muscle groups are involved. Specificity is explicitly distinguished from simulation:
22	"simulation of a sporting movement with small added resistance over the full range of
23	movement or with larger resistance over a restricted part of the movement range may be
24	appropriate at certain stages of training," but "simulation of any movement with
25	significant resistance is inadvisable since it can confuse the neuromuscular programmes"
26	(printed 27), because of changes in center of gravity, moment of inertia, and mechanical
27	stiffness introduced by the resistance. (PDF pp. 38-39, printed pp. 27-28.)
28	
29	**Why it works:** Strength adaptation is produced and expressed by the nervous and
30	muscular systems together (see
31	[[principle--neuromuscular-stimulation-drives-early-strength-gains]]); the specific
32	demands (velocity, joint angle, contraction type, metabolic pathway) shape which
33	recruitment patterns, fibre types, and biochemical pathways are trained, so a change in
34	any one of those parameters can produce a materially different, largely non-transferable
35	adaptation. Inference: the book's own ten-dimension taxonomy and the "little or no
36	improvement on the others" claim are the authors' own framework, not independently
37	established as stated; see
38	[[periodization--bompa/principle--specificity-of-adaptation]] for this library's in-vault
39	discussion of specificity.
40	
41	**When to apply:** **Inference:** usable as a master reasoning check before assuming an
42	exercise "transfers" to a sport skill: ask which of the ten dimensions the exercise
43	actually matches, not just whether it uses similar muscles. **Eric's baseline:** the
44	Principle of Dynamic Correspondence (Verkhoshansky) — matching amplitude/direction of
45	movement, region of force production, dynamics of effort, rate/timing of force production,
46	and regime of muscular work to the sport skill — governs whether an exercise transfers, and
47	is taught in HHPR 5355 (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
48	`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.14`, `week1-lecture.md p.34`). **Inference:**
49	Dynamic Correspondence (this book's Ch4.3, not yet ingested) is plausibly the applied
50	extension of this same ten-dimension specificity logic to exercise selection, though this
51	chapter does not itself state that link.
52	
53	**When NOT to apply:** **Inference:** don't use "specificity" as an argument against any
54	general preparation work; this book's own 1.1 material and this library's Bompa
55	multilateral/LTAD entries support building a general base before narrowing to sport-specific
56	work. This principle governs which dimensions transfer, not whether general work has value
57	at an earlier training age; that distinction is this entry's own reading, not stated as
58	such in this passage of the text.
59	
60	**Example:** **Inference:** Heavy squat strength does not automatically transfer to high-velocity sprint
61	force production (different point on the velocity dimension) even though both use similar
62	musculature; each needs its own specific training exposure.
63	
64	**Related:** [[claim--velocity-and-contraction-specificity-asymmetric-transfer]],
65	[[claim--bilateral-deficit-and-limb-training-specificity]],
66	[[periodization--bompa/principle--specificity-of-adaptation]].

14	# Strength Training Adapts Along (at Least) Ten Independent, Narrow Dimensions
15	
16	**What it is:** Strength gains transfer narrowly, not generally, across at least ten
17	independent dimensions: type of muscle contraction, movement pattern, region/range of
18	movement, velocity of movement, force of contraction, muscle fibre recruitment,
19	metabolism, biochemical adaptation, flexibility, and fatigue. Training that improves one
20	dimension often produces little or no improvement on the others, even when the same
21	muscle groups are involved. Specificity is explicitly distinguished from simulation:
22	"simulation of a sporting movement with small added resistance over the full range of
23	movement or with larger resistance over a restricted part of the movement range may be
24	appropriate at certain stages of training," but "simulation of any movement with
25	significant resistance is inadvisable since it can confuse the neuromuscular programmes"
26	(printed 27), because of changes in center of gravity, moment of inertia, and mechanical
27	stiffness introduced by the resistance. (PDF pp. 38-39, printed pp. 27-28.)
28	
29	**Why it works:** Strength adaptation is produced and expressed by the nervous and
30	muscular systems together (see
31	[[principle--neuromuscular-stimulation-drives-early-strength-gains]]); the specific
32	demands (velocity, joint angle, contraction type, metabolic pathway) shape which
33	recruitment patterns, fibre types, and biochemical pathways are trained, so a change in
34	any one of those parameters can produce a materially different, largely non-transferable
35	adaptation. Inference: the book's own ten-dimension taxonomy and the "little or no
36	improvement on the others" claim are the authors' own framework, not independently
37	established as stated; see
38	[[periodization--bompa/principle--specificity-of-adaptation]] for this library's in-vault
39	discussion of specificity.
40	
41	**When to apply:** **Inference:** usable as a master reasoning check before assuming an
42	exercise "transfers" to a sport skill: ask which of the ten dimensions the exercise
43	actually matches, not just whether it uses similar muscles. **Eric's baseline:** the
44	Principle of Dynamic Correspondence (Verkhoshansky) — matching amplitude/direction of
45	movement, region of force production, dynamics of effort, rate/timing of force production,
46	and regime of muscular work to the sport skill — governs whether an exercise transfers, and
47	is taught in HHPR 5355 (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
48	`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.14`, `week1-lecture.md p.34`). **Inference:**
49	Dynamic Correspondence (this book's Ch4.3, not yet ingested) is plausibly the applied
50	extension of this same ten-dimension specificity logic to exercise selection, though this
51	chapter does not itself state that link.
52	
53	**When NOT to apply:** **Inference:** don't use "specificity" as an argument against any
54	general preparation work; this book's own 1.1 material and this library's Bompa
55	multilateral/LTAD entries support building a general base before narrowing to sport-specific
56	work. This principle governs which dimensions transfer, not whether general work has value
57	at an earlier training age; that distinction is this entry's own reading, not stated as
58	such in this passage of the text.
59	
60	**Example:** **Inference:** Heavy squat strength does not automatically transfer to high-velocity sprint
61	force production (different point on the velocity dimension) even though both use similar
62	musculature; each needs its own specific training exposure.
63	
64	**Related:** [[claim--velocity-and-contraction-specificity-asymmetric-transfer]],
65	[[claim--bilateral-deficit-and-limb-training-specificity]],
66	[[periodization--bompa/principle--specificity-of-adaptation]].

14	# Rate of Force (or Tension) Development Is a Separate Limiter from Maximal Force
15	
16	**What it is:** Sporting performance does not depend simply on the ability to produce
17	maximum force, because many sporting actions happen too fast to recruit an adequate
18	number of muscle fibres in the available time. Rate of Force Development (RFD) / Rate of
19	Tension Development (RTD) — how quickly force rises, not just its ceiling — is named as an
20	independently important limiter, worth assessing on its own alongside maximal-force
21	deficits. (PDF p. 21, printed p. 10; cross-referenced to 2.2.1 for more detail.)
22	
23	**Why it works:** Inference: many athletic actions (sprint ground contact, jump takeoff,
24	change of direction) last far less time than it takes to reach true maximal voluntary
25	force. An athlete can have high 1RM strength but a slow force-time curve, and still
26	underperform in short-duration actions, because the task ends before peak force is reached.
27	This distinction (peak force vs. rate of rise to a sub-maximal time point) is documented in
28	modern force-time curve analysis outside this text (e.g. Maffiuletti et al. 2016, "Rate of
29	force development: physiological and methodological considerations," Eur J Appl Physiol
30	116:1091-1116), which the text itself does not cite.
31	
32	**When to apply:** **Eric's baseline:** force-plate metric selection follows the
33	Output/Driver/Strategy/Fluffy (ODSF) framework, picking 1-2 output metrics, 1-3 driver
34	metrics (e.g. braking/propulsive force), and 1-3 strategy metrics (e.g. phase durations)
35	rather than reporting peak values alone (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and
36	neuromuscular monitoring," citing `hd-odsf-metrics.md`, credited to Hawkin Dynamics, not
37	Eric's own framework). **Inference:** this principle's force-vs-rate distinction supports
38	that driver-metric emphasis and argues for testing and reporting RFD-type variables
39	separately from 1RM or peak-force values, especially for athletes in short-ground-contact
40	positions; this specific link between the ODSF framework and Verkhoshansky's RFD argument
41	is not stated in either source.
42	
43	**When NOT to apply:** **Inference:** don't substitute a single RFD number for the full
44	force-time curve when the movement or time window matters (RFD at 0-50ms is a different
45	quality than RFD at 100-200ms); this time-window caution is this entry's own addition, not
46	stated in this section of the text. The authors cross-reference RFD/RTD deficits to 2.2.1
47	and the strength-deficit discussion to 3.2.1 (PDF p. 21, printed p. 10); Inference: this
48	implies the two qualities are trainable somewhat independently, though the text does not
49	state that implication directly.
50	
51	**Example:** **Inference:** Two athletes with the same back squat 1RM can produce very different sprint
52	starts if one reaches a given force threshold in 100ms and the other takes 200ms; testing
53	and training that difference requires RFD-sensitive measures, not another max-strength
54	test.
55	
56	**Related:** [[heuristic--strength-deficit-sets-training-method-choice]].

14	# Compensatory (Acceleration/Action) Training — Using Proprioceptive Feedback to Actively Manage Bar Speed
15	
16	**What it is:** Free weights (unlike some variable-resistance machines) let the lifter
17	feel changing leverage through the range of motion via proprioceptive feedback and respond
18	by voluntarily accelerating or decelerating the bar to raise or lower the force produced.
19	This is termed Compensatory Acceleration Training (CAT), most obviously used
20	concentrically, but the text argues it applies just as much eccentrically (muscles
21	actively resist gravity's acceleration to control the descent) and even isometrically
22	(the lifter must continuously compensate for fatigue-driven declines in neural drive to
23	hold a constant position), leading the author to prefer "Compensatory Action Training" as
24	the fuller name. (PDF p. 32, printed p. 21; Ch 7.1 develops it further.)
25	
26	**Why it works:** Because force is not fixed by the weight alone (F = ma; a lighter bar
27	accelerated hard can still produce meaningful force), an athlete who actively drives bar
28	speed rather than passively moving a fixed load is directly manipulating the training
29	stimulus at every point in the range of motion, not just at the load's nominal percentage
30	of 1RM.
31	
32	**When to apply:** **Inference:** this reads as a conceptual ancestor of today's
33	velocity-based training (VBT) cueing — "move the bar as fast as possible" instructions on
34	submaximal sets are a modern implementation of the same idea. **Eric's baseline:** Perch
35	camera-based velocity-based training is part of the department's current technology stack
36	(`method-baseline.md`, "Data, technology and reporting," citing
37	`baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7`). **Inference:** CAT's proprioceptive-feedback
38	logic maps onto that existing Perch capability, though neither the book nor the baseline
39	draws this connection directly. **Inference:** also useful as coaching language for
40	eccentric-phase control (actively resisting the descent) and isometric holds (actively
41	maintaining tension); this extension beyond the text's own concentric framing is this
42	entry's own reading of the authors' eccentric/isometric CAT discussion (PDF p. 32,
43	printed p. 21).
44	
45	**When NOT to apply:** **Inference:** this is a technique/cueing concept, not a
46	load-prescription protocol; it doesn't specify a percentage, velocity target, or rep scheme
47	on its own in the text. **Inference:** cueing maximal intended acceleration on every rep is
48	not appropriate for all training goals (e.g., controlled-tempo hypertrophy work
49	deliberately avoids this); this caveat is not addressed in this section of the text.
50	
51	**Example:** **Inference:** Coaching "explode the bar up" on a submaximal front squat set is applying
52	CAT: the athlete voluntarily increases bar acceleration beyond what the load alone would
53	produce, raising the true training force above the load's nominal value.
54

13	
14	# Beginners Respond to Load Alone; Advanced Athletes Need the Full Variable Set
15	
16	**What it is:** Load, reps, and sets are described as the traditional core variables of a
17	weight program, but the text lists a much longer set of variables that matter more as
18	training age rises: the type of strength fitness required, contraction type, movement
19	speed by phase, acceleration at critical points, rest interval length and type
20	(active/passive), exercise sequence,
21	agonist/antagonist and stabilizer/mover strength balance, static/dynamic range of motion,
22	individual strength deficit, training history, injury history, and level of sports
23	proficiency. The proficiency factor is called out as especially important: exact
24	sequencing of strength, strength-speed, and hypertrophy work barely matters in a
25	beginner's first weeks/months but matters a great deal for an experienced athlete. Loads
26	as small as 40% of 1RM can measurably strengthen a beginner but do nothing for an elite
27	athlete. (PDF pp. 22-23, printed pp. 11-12.)
28	
29	**Why it works:** The author gives no mechanism. Inference: a novice's nervous system and
30	tissue are both far from their adaptive ceiling, so almost any consistent stimulus produces
31	a training effect; an advanced athlete has used up most of that low-hanging adaptive room,
32	so the remaining gains depend on precisely managing the variables that were negligible for
33	the novice.
34	
35	**When to apply:** **Inference:** this supports a rule for how much programming detail is
36	worth the coaching time — spend detailed variable-management effort (sequencing, rest
37	structure, ROM, asymmetry work) on advanced/experienced athletes, and keep novice
38	programming simple and consistency-focused. This library's Bompa book makes a related point
39	from the development-model side ([[periodization--bompa/heuristic--biological-vs-training-age|Biological
40	vs Chronological vs Training Age]]), though that entry addresses age-grouping and injury
41	risk rather than this book's programming-variable-complexity angle specifically.
42	
43	**When NOT to apply:** **Inference:** don't use "they're a beginner" as an excuse to
44	ignore movement quality, technique, or safety variables; the text's simplification applies
45	to programming complexity (sequencing, minor load percentages, PDF pp. 22-23, printed pp.
46	11-12), not to coaching attention on how an exercise is performed — this distinction is
47	this entry's own reading, not stated explicitly in the text. **Inference:** an older
48	athlete new to formal training still has a low training age by this logic and should be
49	treated as a beginner by this rule, not by chronological age; the text does not
50	draw that chronological-vs-training-age distinction itself in this section.
51	
52	**Example:** **Inference:** A true freshman gains strength on almost any structured 3x/week program with
53	straightforward load progression; a fourth-year starter needs exercise sequencing,
54	recovery structure, and asymmetry correction actively managed to keep progressing.
55	
56	**Related:** [[framework--resistance-training-prescription-by-goal]].
57

14	# Rate of Force (or Tension) Development Is a Separate Limiter from Maximal Force
15	
16	**What it is:** Sporting performance does not depend simply on the ability to produce
17	maximum force, because many sporting actions happen too fast to recruit an adequate
18	number of muscle fibres in the available time. Rate of Force Development (RFD) / Rate of
19	Tension Development (RTD) — how quickly force rises, not just its ceiling — is named as an
20	independently important limiter, worth assessing on its own alongside maximal-force
21	deficits. (PDF p. 21, printed p. 10; cross-referenced to 2.2.1 for more detail.)
22	
23	**Why it works:** Inference: many athletic actions (sprint ground contact, jump takeoff,
24	change of direction) last far less time than it takes to reach true maximal voluntary
25	force. An athlete can have high 1RM strength but a slow force-time curve, and still
26	underperform in short-duration actions, because the task ends before peak force is reached.
27	This distinction (peak force vs. rate of rise to a sub-maximal time point) is documented in
28	modern force-time curve analysis outside this text (e.g. Maffiuletti et al. 2016, "Rate of
29	force development: physiological and methodological considerations," Eur J Appl Physiol
30	116:1091-1116), which the text itself does not cite.
31	
32	**When to apply:** **Eric's baseline:** force-plate metric selection follows the
33	Output/Driver/Strategy/Fluffy (ODSF) framework, picking 1-2 output metrics, 1-3 driver
34	metrics (e.g. braking/propulsive force), and 1-3 strategy metrics (e.g. phase durations)
35	rather than reporting peak values alone (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and
36	neuromuscular monitoring," citing `hd-odsf-metrics.md`, credited to Hawkin Dynamics, not
37	Eric's own framework). **Inference:** this principle's force-vs-rate distinction supports
38	that driver-metric emphasis and argues for testing and reporting RFD-type variables
39	separately from 1RM or peak-force values, especially for athletes in short-ground-contact
40	positions; this specific link between the ODSF framework and Verkhoshansky's RFD argument
41	is not stated in either source.
42	
43	**When NOT to apply:** **Inference:** don't substitute a single RFD number for the full
44	force-time curve when the movement or time window matters (RFD at 0-50ms is a different
45	quality than RFD at 100-200ms); this time-window caution is this entry's own addition, not
46	stated in this section of the text. The authors cross-reference RFD/RTD deficits to 2.2.1
47	and the strength-deficit discussion to 3.2.1 (PDF p. 21, printed p. 10); Inference: this
48	implies the two qualities are trainable somewhat independently, though the text does not
49	state that implication directly.
50	
51	**Example:** **Inference:** Two athletes with the same back squat 1RM can produce very different sprint
52	starts if one reaches a given force threshold in 100ms and the other takes 200ms; testing
53	and training that difference requires RFD-sensitive measures, not another max-strength
54	test.
55	
56	**Related:** [[heuristic--strength-deficit-sets-training-method-choice]].
57

# Table 1.1 — Resistance Training Prescription by Goal (Strength, Power, Hypertrophy, Endurance)

**What it is:** A dynamic (non-isometric) resistance-training prescription chart by
goal (PDF p. 22, printed p. 11):

| Variable | Strength | Power | Hypertrophy | Endurance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Load (% 1RM) | 80-100 | 70-100 | 60-80 | 40-60 |
| Reps/set | 1-5 | 1-5 | 8-15 | 25-60 |
| Sets/exercise | 4-7 | 3-5 | 4-8 | 2-4 |
| Rest between sets | 2-6 min | 2-6 min | 2-5 min | 1-2 min |
| Duration/set | 5-10 s | 4-8 s | 20-60 s | 80-150 s |
| Speed/rep (% max) | 60-100 | 90-100 | 60-90 | 6-80 (as printed; probably a misprint for 60-80) |
| Sessions/week | 3-6 | 3-6 | 5-7 | 8-14 |

High-volume, low-resistance work is called an **extensive** method (an
**extensification/accumulation** phase); low-volume, high-intensity work is an
**intensive** method (an **intensification** phase). Early training typically opens with
an extensive phase before progressing to an intensive one; periodization is described as
cyclically alternating these two phase types.

**Why it works:** The author gives no mechanism for the table itself. Inference: each goal
loads the neuromuscular and metabolic systems differently: near-maximal loads at low reps
bias neural recruitment and force capacity (strength); high-velocity submaximal loads bias
rate of force development (power); moderate loads at moderate-to-high volume bias metabolic
and mechanical stress for hypertrophy; light loads at very high reps bias oxidative/
metabolic endurance.

**When to apply:** **Inference:** usable as a first-pass, generic reference when scoping a
new program's load/volume targets by goal, and as shared vocabulary for extensive/intensive
phase naming. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355 already teaches undulating/non-linear
periodization (Parker/Miller/Panariello), waving volume week to week, stated as the
personally preferred model over strict linear progression (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength
and power," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.24-26`). **Inference:** that
undulating model and this text's extensive/intensive phase language describe related but
not identical ideas (wave-to-wave volume change vs. phase-to-phase intensity change); the
baseline material does not cite the book's specific terminology.

**When NOT to apply:** The authors state this chart is "adequate for the average
personal trainer or coach dealing with the average client or lower level athlete" but
incomplete for advanced athletes: it ignores strength-speed, explosive strength,
flexibility-strength, and strength-endurance as separate qualities (PDF p. 21, printed p.
10; the "average personal trainer" quote is PDF p. 22, printed p. 11), and ignores the other
prescription variables covered in
[[heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age]] and later chapters.

not use this table as a complete program design tool for a well-trained collegiate
athlete; treat it as a starting reference, not an endpoint.

adjustments the text says this table omits.

17	ladder of distinct maxima, from lowest to highest: training maximum (TFmax, the training
18	1RM, the heaviest load one can lift without a large emotional/heart-rate spike),
19	competitive maximum (CFmax, the true 1RM produced under optimal competitive motivation),
20	and absolute strength (Fmm, "maximum of all maxima," the involuntary ceiling reachable
21	only under electrical stimulation or a sudden reflex-recruited load, e.g. a sudden drop
22	or stretch reflex). Relative strength is strength per unit bodymass for a given lift.
23	Voluntary maxima also rank by contraction type, in order of magnitude: eccentric >
24	isometric > concentric. (PDF pp. 12-13, printed pp. 1-2.)
25	
26	**Why it works:** Nervous system inhibition (protective feedback, comparable to a
27	mechanical governor) normally prevents a muscle from contracting to the point of
28	structural failure. Competitive arousal and motivation reduce that inhibition further
29	than routine training effort does, which is why CFmax exceeds TFmax; involuntary or
30	reflex-driven recruitment removes still more of it, which is why Fmm exceeds CFmax.
31	
32	**When to apply:** The authors state the competitive maximum, not the daily training
33	maximum, should set %-based intensity zones for higher-level athletes, because CFmax stays
34	comparatively stable while TFmax fluctuates day to day (PDF p. 13, printed p. 2).
35	**Inference:** this ladder is a useful lens for deciding which measured maximum should
36	anchor programmed intensity for a given athlete. **Eric's baseline:** velocity-based 1RM
37	estimation (linear-displacement transducer, target mean velocity) is preferred over live
38	1RM attempts to avoid the fatigue and injury risk of true maxing (`method-baseline.md`,

45	not itself named in the baseline material as the current 1RM-estimation tool.
46	
47	**When NOT to apply:** This is a terminology and reasoning framework, not a measured
48	protocol; Fmm requires electrical stimulation or reflex loading, which the text
49	calls impractical (PDF p. 12, printed p. 1). **Inference:** none of these four
50	maxima are named as routinely and directly measured in Baylor's own documented protocols
51	(`method-baseline.md`), so this should be treated as a mental model for why training-day
52	and competition-day 1RMs diverge, not as a set of numbers to test for. The text gives the
53	eccentric > isometric > concentric ordering "as a matter of interest" (printed 2) without
54	stating it is a fixed ratio; Inference: it likely varies by joint angle, velocity, and
55	muscle group, though the text does not make that qualification in this passage.

58	what they hit in a max-out competition or meet (CFmax); programming off the meet number

60	competitive performance.

14	# Central vs. Peripheral Fatigue, and Low- vs. High-Frequency Fatigue
15	
16	**What it is:** Fatigue during short-duration strength/power work is split into
17	**central fatigue** (reduced motivation, impaired spinal nerve transmission, reduced motor
18	neuron recruitment and firing rate — a CNS-level phenomenon) and **peripheral fatigue**
19	(failure somewhere in the excitation-contraction chain at the muscle cell itself: motor
20	end-plate, sarcolemma, T-tubules, sarcoplasmic reticulum, contractile proteins).
21	Peripheral fatigue further splits into **low-frequency fatigue** (impaired force at <20 Hz
22	stimulation, from depressed calcium release, with a prolonged recovery period "persisting
23	for as long as 48 hours," printed 15) and **high-frequency fatigue** (impaired force at
24	>50 Hz; the text gives no recovery-speed comparison between the two, printed 14-15).
25	Two distinct purposes are given for reduced central drive during fatigue, on different
26	pages: for short-term maximal contractions, the reduction in motor-neuron firing rate "may
27	be beneficial in avoiding electrical failure and facilitating maximal mechanical response"
28	(printed 15); separately, "muscle wisdom," the CNS's down-regulation of motor neuron
29	discharge rate during a sustained contraction, has a purpose "believed to ensure that
30	central neural drive to fatigued skeletal muscle matches that which is needed to generate
31	the required force," and "may be one mechanism that functions either to decrease or to
32	postpone central neural fatigue" (printed 16). Exercise-induced ammonia accumulation is
33	cited as a possible contributor to central fatigue at high intensities/durations. Intensive
34	CNS activation (max weights, max power, plyometrics) is stated to need at least 48 hours of
35	recovery if no restorative methods are used. (PDF pp. 24-27, printed pp. 13-16.)
36	
37	**Why it works:** Inference: fatigue is not a single process with one cause; the
38	central/peripheral split and the frequency-dependent split reflect genuinely different
39	physiological bottlenecks (nervous drive vs. contractile-machinery failure vs.
40	calcium-handling kinetics), which is why they have different time courses.
41	
42	**When to apply:** The authors state intensive CNS activation (max weights, max power,
43	plyometrics) needs at least 48 hours of recovery if no restorative methods are used (PDF p.
44	26, printed p. 15). **Inference:** this supports spacing high-CNS-cost sessions (max
45	strength, high-velocity work) at least two days apart within a microcycle, and treating
46	"still feels flat two days after a max-effort day" as plausible central fatigue rather than
47	assuming poor effort or motivation; this specific practical framing is not stated in the
48	text.
49	
50	**When NOT to apply:** **Inference:** this is a mechanistic taxonomy from exercise
51	physiology, not a monitoring protocol. **Eric's baseline:** modified reactive strength
52	index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing is the department's chosen daily readiness marker
53	(`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
54	`2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`); **Inference:** mRSI is a downstream readiness proxy,
55	not a direct central/peripheral fatigue assay, so a flat CMJ day should not be
56	over-attributed to a specific named mechanism (e.g., "low-frequency fatigue") without EMG
57	or stimulation data — neither source states this equivalence, and this caution is this
58	entry's own judgment.
59	
60	**Example:** Inference: a depressed CMJ the day after max squats more likely reflects
61	residual fatigue than lost strength; retest at 48 hours rather than reacting to a single
62	depressed value.
63	
64	**Related:** [[framework--factors-limiting-strength-production]].

13	
14	# Functional vs. Structural Resistance Training
15	
16	**What it is:** Two basic categories of resistance training effect: structural training
17	targets muscle hypertrophy (and some tissue flexibility); functional training targets
18	performance qualities (static strength, speed-strength, muscular endurance, reactive
19	ability) through four neural mechanisms: (1) intermuscular coordination — sequencing and
20	synchronizing action between different muscle groups; (2) intramuscular coordination —
21	control within one muscle via number encoding (how many fibres are recruited), rate
22	encoding (firing frequency), and pattern encoding (sequencing of fibre types); (3)
23	facilitatory/inhibitory reflex processes; (4) motor learning, programming the CNS to
24	execute a specific task. No training is purely structural; all training is functional to
25	some degree and may also elicit structural change. (PDF p. 18, printed p. 7.)
26	
27	**Why it works:** The authors state the sequence ("in the early stages of training or
28	during stagnation at an advanced level, the functional stages should precede the
29	structural stages," printed 8) but give no mechanism for it. Inference: force output for a
30	given movement is the product of both how much contractile tissue exists (structural) and
31	how effectively the nervous system recruits, times, and sequences that tissue (functional).
32	Early or stagnation-phase training may get more return from the functional side because
33	coordination has more room to improve; structural change is slower and more load-dependent.
34	
35	**When to apply:** The authors state functional stages should precede structural
36	stages both for beginners and during a plateau at an advanced level (PDF p. 19, printed p.
37	8, cross-referenced to 1.2 and Ch2). **Inference:** this supports using the split as a
38	diagnostic lens when an athlete's strength stalls: ask whether the limiter is likely
39	structural (needs more hypertrophy-phase volume) or functional (needs improved
40	coordination, rate coding, or motor learning of the specific lift/skill); this diagnostic
41	framing is this entry's own extension, not stated as a test procedure in the text.
42	
43	**When NOT to apply:** **Inference:** this is a conceptual split, not a measured
44	diagnostic; number, rate, and pattern encoding are not directly observable from a force
45	plate or barbell velocity alone, so inferring which mechanism is limiting a given athlete
46	is coach judgment, not a test result. The authors' use of "functional training" here
47	means neural coordination and recruitment specifically (PDF p. 18, printed p. 7);
48	**Inference:** don't confuse it with the modern commercial-gym use of the same term
49	(balance boards, unstable surfaces), which is a different, later usage the text does not
50	address.
51	
52	**Example:** **Inference:** A lifter whose 1RM is stagnant despite visible muscle gain may be limited by
53	intermuscular coordination (poor bracing/synchronization under heavy load) rather than by
54	insufficient muscle; technique and coordination work, not more volume, is the higher-value
55	fix.
56	
57	**Related:** [[principle--neuromuscular-stimulation-drives-early-strength-gains]].
58

13	
14	# The Force-Velocity Relationship, and Why Strength Doesn't Guarantee Speed
15	
16	**What it is:** Hill's hyperbolic force-velocity curve: velocity of contraction is
17	inversely related to load; large force cannot be produced at very high velocities under
18	constant conditions; heavy strength training shifts the curve upward, particularly in
19	beginners (raising force at all velocities, called training for "strength-speed"); light,
20	high-velocity training shifts the curve's velocity maximum rightward (called training for
21	"speed-strength"). Because power = force x velocity, both shifts raise power, just at
22	different points on the curve. Zatsiorsky (1995) reports "there is no correlation between
23	maximal velocity and maximal strength" (printed 20); the ability to generate maximum
24	strength and to produce high speed are described as different motor abilities. Inference:
25	this specific claim is contested by modern data (Wisloff et al. 2004, Br J Sports Med
26	38:285, squat 1RM vs. 10 m sprint time, r ~0.94; Seitz et al. 2014, Sports Med, strength
27	gains transferring to sprint performance). (PDF pp. 30-31, printed pp. 19-20; Zatsiorsky &
28	Matveev 1964, Komi 1979, Zatsiorsky 1995.)
29	
30	**Why it works:** The Hill curve, "although this relationship originally was derived for
31	isolated muscle, ... has been confirmed for actual sporting movement" (printed 19). Beyond
32	that author's statement, the rest is Inference: the F-V relationship reflects the
33	cross-bridge cycling and motor unit recruitment limits of muscle contraction, and is the
34	conceptual ancestor of the force-velocity profiling methods (Samozino, Morin, and others)
35	used in modern sprint and jump testing; the book does not itself draw that connection to
36	modern profiling.
37
