# The Force-Velocity Relationship, and Why Strength Doesn't Guarantee Speed

**What it is:** Hill's hyperbolic force-velocity curve: velocity of contraction is
inversely related to load; large force cannot be produced at very high velocities under
constant conditions; heavy strength training shifts the curve upward, particularly in
beginners (raising force at all velocities, called training for "strength-speed"); light,
high-velocity training shifts the curve's velocity maximum rightward (called training for
"speed-strength"). Because power = force x velocity, both shifts raise power, just at
different points on the curve. Zatsiorsky (1995) reports "there is no correlation between
maximal velocity and maximal strength" (printed 20); the ability to generate maximum
strength and to produce high speed are described as different motor abilities. Inference:
this specific claim is contested by modern data (Wisloff et al. 2004, Br J Sports Med
38:285, squat 1RM vs. 10 m sprint time, r ~0.94; Seitz et al. 2014, Sports Med, strength
gains transferring to sprint performance). (PDF pp. 30-31, printed pp. 19-20; Zatsiorsky &
Matveev 1964, Komi 1979, Zatsiorsky 1995.)

**Why it works:** The Hill curve, "although this relationship originally was derived for
isolated muscle, ... has been confirmed for actual sporting movement" (printed 19). Beyond
that author's statement, the rest is Inference: the F-V relationship reflects the
cross-bridge cycling and motor unit recruitment limits of muscle contraction, and is the
conceptual ancestor of the force-velocity profiling methods (Samozino, Morin, and others)
used in modern sprint and jump testing; the book does not itself draw that connection to
modern profiling.

the force-velocity spectrum rather than assuming "more strength" automatically transfers to

14	# Strength Training Adapts Along (at Least) Ten Independent, Narrow Dimensions
15	
16	**What it is:** Strength gains transfer narrowly, not generally, across at least ten
17	independent dimensions: type of muscle contraction, movement pattern, region/range of
18	movement, velocity of movement, force of contraction, muscle fibre recruitment,
19	metabolism, biochemical adaptation, flexibility, and fatigue. Training that improves one
20	dimension often produces little or no improvement on the others, even when the same
21	muscle groups are involved. Specificity is explicitly distinguished from simulation:
22	"simulation of a sporting movement with small added resistance over the full range of
23	movement or with larger resistance over a restricted part of the movement range may be
24	appropriate at certain stages of training," but "simulation of any movement with
25	significant resistance is inadvisable since it can confuse the neuromuscular programmes"
26	(printed 27), because of changes in center of gravity, moment of inertia, and mechanical
27	stiffness introduced by the resistance. (PDF pp. 38-39, printed pp. 27-28.)
28	
29	**Why it works:** Strength adaptation is produced and expressed by the nervous and
30	muscular systems together (see
31	[[principle--neuromuscular-stimulation-drives-early-strength-gains]]); the specific
32	demands (velocity, joint angle, contraction type, metabolic pathway) shape which
33	recruitment patterns, fibre types, and biochemical pathways are trained, so a change in
34	any one of those parameters can produce a materially different, largely non-transferable
35	adaptation. Inference: the book's own ten-dimension taxonomy and the "little or no
36	improvement on the others" claim are the authors' own framework, not independently
37	established as stated; see
38	[[periodization--bompa/principle--specificity-of-adaptation]] for this library's in-vault
39	discussion of specificity.

42	exercise "transfers" to a sport skill: ask which of the ten dimensions the exercise
43	actually matches, not just whether it uses similar muscles. **Eric's baseline:** the
44	Principle of Dynamic Correspondence (Verkhoshansky) — matching amplitude/direction of
45	movement, region of force production, dynamics of effort, rate/timing of force production,
46	and regime of muscular work to the sport skill — governs whether an exercise transfers, and

48	`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.14`, `week1-lecture.md p.34`). **Inference:**
49	Dynamic Correspondence (this book's Ch4.3, not yet ingested) is plausibly the applied
50	extension of this same ten-dimension specificity logic to exercise selection, though this
51	chapter does not itself state that link.

53	**When NOT to apply:** **Inference:** don't use "specificity" as an argument against any
54	general preparation work; this book's own 1.1 material and this library's Bompa

56	work. This principle governs which dimensions transfer, not whether general work has value
57	at an earlier training age; that distinction is this entry's own reading, not stated as

15	
16	**What it is:** Verkhoshansky (citing Zatsiorsky) defines three related but distinct

18	intensity and duration using its energy systems. Fitness is the specific ability to use
19	that work capacity to execute a given task efficiently and safely; it is a slow-changing
20	state that does not vary meaningfully over a period of days. Preparedness is not stable:
21	it is the resultant, at any given instant, of the interaction between the slow-changing
22	fitness component and the fast-changing, opposing effect of exercise-induced fatigue.
23	"Instantaneous preparedness" can be pushed down by transient factors (mental state,
24	sickness, fatigue, sleepiness) without any change in underlying fitness. (PDF pp. 43-44,
25	printed pp. 32-33; developed further at 1.16.3.)

28	state-dependent expression of it (preparedness) explains why an athlete's fitness can be
29	objectively unchanged from one day to the next while their measured or perceived output
30	still swings substantially, because the fatigue component is riding on top of a stable

38	closely onto this framework's fitness/preparedness split (fitness ~ the baseline's

49	(fitness/base preparedness) have been stable for weeks can still show a depressed CMJ

13	
14	# Structural and Functional Determinants of Strength
15	
16	**What it is:** The authors list the factors that determine how much strength a
17	muscle group can produce. Structural factors: cross-sectional area of the muscle, density
18	of fibres per unit cross-section, and mechanical leverage efficiency across the joint.
19	Functional (neural) factors: number of fibres contracting simultaneously, rate of fibre
20	contraction, efficiency of firing synchronization, nerve conduction velocity, degree of
21	inhibition of non-contributing fibres, proportion of large-diameter (fast-twitch) fibres
22	active, efficiency of cooperation between fibre types, efficiency of stretch reflexes,
23	excitation threshold of the nerve fibres, and initial muscle length before contraction.
24	Maximum strength is produced at an optimum, not a maximum, frequency of nerve firing
25	(Vredensky, via Vorobyev 1978), and that optimal frequency itself shifts with fatigue
26	level (Kernell & Monster, 1982). Synchronization of motor unit firing across fibres does
27	not appear to meaningfully increase the rate of strength production; sequencing
28	(efficient timing) may matter more than simultaneity, especially where stored elastic
29	energy must be released at the right moment (Miller et al., 1981). (PDF pp. 44-45,
30	printed pp. 33-34.)
31	
32	**Why it works:** This is a fuller inventory of why two athletes with the same
33	cross-sectional muscle area can produce very different force: most of the list is neural
34	(recruitment, timing, inhibition, reflex efficiency), consistent with this chapter's
35	overall theme that strength is a neuromuscular, not purely structural, phenomenon.
36

# Structural and Functional Determinants of Strength

**What it is:** The authors list the factors that determine how much strength a
muscle group can produce. Structural factors: cross-sectional area of the muscle, density
of fibres per unit cross-section, and mechanical leverage efficiency across the joint.
Functional (neural) factors: number of fibres contracting simultaneously, rate of fibre
contraction, efficiency of firing synchronization, nerve conduction velocity, degree of
inhibition of non-contributing fibres, proportion of large-diameter (fast-twitch) fibres
active, efficiency of cooperation between fibre types, efficiency of stretch reflexes,
excitation threshold of the nerve fibres, and initial muscle length before contraction.
Maximum strength is produced at an optimum, not a maximum, frequency of nerve firing
(Vredensky, via Vorobyev 1978), and that optimal frequency itself shifts with fatigue
level (Kernell & Monster, 1982). Synchronization of motor unit firing across fibres does
not appear to meaningfully increase the rate of strength production; sequencing
(efficient timing) may matter more than simultaneity, especially where stored elastic
energy must be released at the right moment (Miller et al., 1981). (PDF pp. 44-45,
printed pp. 33-34.)

**Why it works:** This is a fuller inventory of why two athletes with the same
cross-sectional muscle area can produce very different force: most of the list is neural
(recruitment, timing, inhibition, reflex efficiency), consistent with this chapter's
overall theme that strength is a neuromuscular, not purely structural, phenomenon.

**When to apply:** **Inference:** useful as a longer checklist than
[[framework--functional-vs-structural-resistance-training]] when explaining to students
or staff (e.g. in HHPR 5355) why hypertrophy alone does not fully predict strength, and
for generating hypotheses about why an athlete with good muscle mass underperforms on
force output (check firing rate, synchronization, initial muscle length/joint angle,
rather than assuming a training-volume problem).

**When NOT to apply:** The authors note more research is needed before drawing a
firm conclusion about strength gains from increased motor-unit synchronization (PDF p.
45, printed p. 34); **Inference:** do not treat "improve synchronization" as an
established, targetable training goal on its own — none of these functional factors
listed have a stated field-testable metric in this section.

**Example:** **Inference:** two athletes with similar squat cross-sectional muscle
estimates (e.g. via anthropometrics) but different 1RM outputs are most likely differing
on the functional/neural list (recruitment, firing rate, inhibition), not on structural
factors alone.

**Related:** [[framework--functional-vs-structural-resistance-training]],
[[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]].

14	# Collagenous Tissue's Four-Region Loading Curve, and Why Loading Rate Changes What Fails First
15	
16	**What it is:** Collagenous tissue (e.g. the ACL, studied by Frankel & Nordin 1980)
17	loaded to failure shows four regions: Region I, the "toe region," where the crimped
18	tissue straightens with little force and mild stretching here produces no long-term
19	flexibility change; Region II, a near-linear region where fibres are fully uncrimped and
20	parallel; Region III, where sequential microfailure of overstretched fibres begins; Region
21	IV, complete failure. Loading rate changes the outcome: increasing loading rate roughly
22	fourfold raised knee ligament failure load by almost 50% (Kennedy et al., 1976), and which
23	structure fails first flips with rate — at slow loading rates the ligament's bony
24	insertion is the weakest link, while at fast loading rates the ligament itself is the
25	weakest link (bone's strength rises faster with rate than the ligament's). Healthy tendon's
26	tensile strength can be more than twice that of its associated muscle, which is why
27	ruptures are more common in muscle than tendon. (PDF pp. 54-56, printed pp. 43-45.)
28	
29	**Why it works:** Collagen is viscoelastic: it behaves more elastically under rapid
30	loading and more plastically (creeping, deforming) under slow, sustained loading, so both
31	the loading speed and the tissue's own rate-dependent stiffness change determine where in
32	the body an excessive load actually causes failure.
33	
34	**When to apply:** **Inference:** relevant background for understanding why static
35	stretching held gently (Region I) does not meaningfully change tissue length or
36	flexibility over time, and why ballistic or rapid loading, once past Region II, carries
37	real microfailure risk; also relevant context for why the pattern of injury (bone
38	avulsion vs. mid-ligament tear vs. muscle strain) can differ by the speed of the loading
39	event, which matters for how Athletic Medicine and Applied Performance jointly interpret
40	an injury mechanism.
41	
42	**When NOT to apply:** **Inference:** this is basic tissue mechanics from cited
43	1970s-1980s cadaveric/animal ligament research, not a live-tissue, in-vivo human athlete
44	dataset; do not use the specific numbers (50% failure-load increase, the fourfold rate
45	figure) as applicable outside the original knee-ligament loading-rate study (Kennedy 1976,
46	printed 44); only the strain curve (Fig 1.21) is specifically ACL.
47	This is background science, not a clinical decision rule, and should not substitute for
48	Athletic Medicine's own injury assessment framework.
49	
50	**Example:** **Inference:** a sudden high-rate valgus load to the knee is more likely to
51	produce mid-ligament ACL failure, while a slower, sustained load is more likely to fail at
52	the bony insertion first; this pattern helps explain, but does not replace, imaging and
53	clinical exam in determining actual injury location.
54	
55	**Related:** [[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]],
56	[[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]].

14	# The Muscle Model: Series Elastic Component (SEC) vs. Parallel Elastic Component (PEC)
15	
16	**What it is:** A mechanical model of muscle (Levin & Wyman, 1927) treats it as a
17	contractile component in series with a Series Elastic Component (SEC: tendon,
18	cross-bridges, myofilaments, titin, Z-discs) and in parallel with a Parallel Elastic
19	Component (PEC: sarcolemma, rest-state cross-bridging, surrounding sheaths). The PEC
20	carries the force of a relaxed muscle stretched beyond resting length, and stores little
21	usable energy; the SEC is tensioned by an actively contracting muscle resisting a rapid
22	stretch, and stores considerable elastic energy — this is the mechanism plyometric/shock
23	training exploits. Slow-twitch (ST) dominant muscle shows smaller mechanical strain when
24	stretched while contracted but has a stiffer, more elastic SEC than fast-twitch
25	(FT)-dominant muscle, largely due to higher collagen concentration in slow muscle. The book
26	gives conflicting statements on which fibre type stores more elastic energy overall:
27	printed 41 states "the stored elastic energy is greater in FT fibres" (Komi, 1984), while
28	printed 46 states "a slow muscle can store relatively more elastic energy in its
29	collagenous tissue than fast muscle." Both are recorded here rather than harmonized.
30	Static, relaxed, and passive stretching mainly load the PEC; "tense ballistic and active
31	stretching affects predominantly the SEC," while PNF techniques "appear to be able to
32	stretch and strengthen both the SEC and the PEC" (printed 41-42). (PDF pp. 51-53, 57;
33	printed pp. 40-42, 46.)
34	
35	**Why it works:** Inference: knowing which component (PEC or SEC) is under tension in a
36	given stretch or contraction explains why static/passive and active/PNF stretching target
37	different tissue; the book conflicts on which fibre type stores more elastic energy
38	(printed 41 vs. 46), so no single fibre-type/component pairing can be asserted as the
39	mechanism.
40	
41	**When to apply:** **Inference:** useful for explaining why plyometric/reactive-strength
42	training targets the SEC specifically (rapid stretch under active contraction) rather than
43	simple static flexibility work (which mostly loads the PEC), and for choosing PNF-style
44	active stretching when the goal is to influence both components rather than the PEC alone.
45	
46	**When NOT to apply:** **Inference:** the anatomical location of SEC/PEC elements is
47	explicitly stated as not precisely identified (PDF p. 52, printed p. 41); treat this as a
48	functional/mechanical model for reasoning about elastic energy, not a literal anatomical
49	map to test or measure directly in an athlete.
50	
51	**Example:** Inference: by the authors' own account, slow postural muscle needs longer
52	stretching to meaningfully change its flexibility than fast muscle does (printed 41), which
53	supports muscle-specific rather than uniform flexibility prescription; this is distinct
54	from, and does not depend on, the unresolved FT-vs-ST elastic-energy-storage conflict
55	above.
56	
57	**Related:** [[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]],
58	[[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]].

14	# Precise Muscle-Action Terminology: Why "Isotonic" and "Isokinetic" Are Usually Wrong
15	
16	**What it is:** The authors argue most everyday strength-training terms are
17	technically imprecise. Concentric: proximal and distal muscle attachments move toward one
18	another. Eccentric: they move apart (not literally a "contraction," despite the common
19	name — the muscle is returning toward resting length under load). Isometric: attachments
20	don't move relative to each other (joint angle constant); more accurately called "static."
21	"Isotonic" (constant tension) is argued to be almost never actually true during real joint
22	movement, since tension changes with acceleration, deceleration, and reflex activation
23	throughout a range; European and Russian scientists prefer "auxotonic" (changing tension
24	and length) or "allodynamic" instead. "Isokinetic" (constant velocity) is also argued to
25	be physically impossible over a full range, since starting from and returning to rest
26	requires acceleration; isokinetic devices are more accurately "quasi-isokinetic," and
27	isokinetic-machine torque output is typically much lower than isometric torque at the same
28	joint angle. "Quasi-isometric" action is defined separately: the slow, near-static muscle
29	action seen in heavy, near-maximal resistance training performed anywhere across a joint's
30	range (not fixed at one angle like true isometrics), relevant to maximal strength,
31	hypertrophy, and active flexibility training rather than power or speed. (PDF pp. 60-64,
32	printed pp. 49-53.)
33	
34	**Why it works:** Real joint movement always involves changing acceleration
35	(Newton's laws), so any term implying a truly constant mechanical variable throughout a
36	full range is describing an idealization, not the actual muscle physics; the more precise
37	terms track what is actually held constant and where.
38	
39	**When to apply:** **Inference:** relevant when interpreting or reporting isokinetic
40	dynamometer data (if used by Athletic Medicine or research collaborators): understand that
41	the constant-velocity claim applies only to the device's controlled range, not to the
42	underlying muscle action, and that isokinetic torque values are not directly comparable to
43	isometric (e.g. IMTP) values at the same joint angle. Also useful coaching-language
44	precision: heavy squat/bench-style lifting performed slowly is "quasi-isometric," a
45	distinct quality from true fixed-angle isometrics like the IMTP.
46	
47	**When NOT to apply:** **Inference:** this is a terminology-precision argument, not a
48	claim that isokinetic or isotonic training methods are ineffective; the critique is about
49	what the words accurately describe, not about training value. Don't over-correct common
50	usage in casual coaching communication where the imprecise terms are well understood by
51	convention.
52	
53	**Example:** **Inference:** describing an IMTP as "isometric" (fixed joint angle) versus
54	a slow, heavy back squat as "quasi-isometric" (near-static but occurring across a range)
55	keeps clear which type of force-plate or barbell data is actually comparable to which.
56	
57	**Related:** [[principle--triphasic-nature-of-muscle-action]].
58

13	
14	# All Dynamic Movement Is Triphasic: Isometric, Then Concentric/Eccentric, Then Isometric Again
15	
16	**What it is:** Classifying muscle action as simply "static" (isometric) or "dynamic"
17	(concentric/eccentric) is described as an oversimplification. Every dynamic action must
18	begin from an isometric phase (the muscle must first develop enough tension to
19	counterbalance the load before any movement starts: concentric if tension exceeds the
20	load, eccentric if it doesn't), and every movement ends in another isometric phase before
21	reversing or stopping, because Newton's laws require the system to momentarily come to
22	rest at a direction change. In ballistic/ fast movement, the transition isometric phase is
23	very brief; in slow maximal efforts (e.g. a powerlifting squat or bench), it can be much
24	longer. The brief isometric phase in a plyometric movement is specifically termed
25	"explosive isometric" action and is central to speed-strength training and movements like
26	the weightlifting jerk, shot put, and high jump. Movement termination/reversal can also
27	involve any combination of agonist eccentric or isometric action, antagonist concentric or
28	isometric action, stabilizer action at the joint or nearby joints, and passive connective-
29	tissue damping — not simply "antagonist opposes agonist" as popular descriptions suggest.
30	(PDF pp. 65-66, printed pp. 54-55.)
31	
32	**Why it works:** This follows directly from Newtonian mechanics (a moving system must
33	have zero velocity at the instant it reverses direction) combined with the physiological
34	fact that muscle tension must build before it can move a load; the "explosive isometric"
35	phase is the same brief coupling window discussed in
36	[[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]], described here from the
37	whole-joint-action perspective rather than the cross-bridge perspective.
38	
39	**When to apply:** **Inference:** reinforces that "isometric strength" is not a separate,
40	niche quality but a phase present in every dynamic lift and sprint/jump action, which
41	supports including isometric testing (IMTP) and isometric-emphasis training as directly
42	relevant to dynamic performance, not a side quality. Also a caution for kinesiology
43	teaching (e.g. HHPR 5355): movement termination is not simply "antagonist stops agonist";
44	several structures can share that role, so a simplistic agonist/antagonist explanation for
45	a given movement's braking phase may be incomplete.
46	
47	**When NOT to apply:** The text itself notes inappropriate antagonist activation
48	opposing a strongly contracting agonist is a recognized injury mechanism (e.g. hamstrings
49	rupturing when they fire to oppose the quadriceps during sprinting or kicking, PDF p. 60,
50	printed p. 49); **Inference:** this triphasic framework describes normal, coordinated
51	movement termination, and should not be conflated with that pathological
52	premature-antagonist-activation injury pattern, which is a distinct, unwanted phenomenon
53	rather than part of the normal triphasic sequence.
54	
55	**Example:** **Inference:** a sprinter's ground-contact phase is not purely
56	"eccentric-then-concentric"; it necessarily includes the brief isometric coupling phase
57	this principle describes, which is the same window where the reactive-strength/elastic
58	mechanism in [[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]] operates.
59	
60	**Related:** [[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]],
61	[[framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology]].

14	# The S-Factors Pyramidal Model of Fitness (Strength, Speed, Stamina, Suppleness, Skill, Structure, Spirit)
15	
16	**What it is:** A comprehensive model of fitness built from seven "S-factors": Strength,
17	Speed, Stamina (systemic or local muscular endurance), Suppleness (flexibility), Skill
18	(neuromuscular efficiency, including a "Style" sub-quality — an individual's manner of
19	expressing a skill), Structure (somatotype, size, shape), and Spirit (psychological
20	preparedness). The model is built in two stages: a triangular base relating strength,
21	stamina, speed, and suppleness, then a pyramid adding skill/neuromuscular control as the
22	process that makes all movement possible, with flexibility placed at the center of the
23	base because range of movement underlies expression of every other quality. From the
24	pairwise relationships between factors, an extended list of compound fitness qualities is
25	derived: static/dynamic strength and strength-endurance, strength-speed, speed-strength,
26	speed-strength endurance, strength-speed endurance, speed, endurance, flexibility-strength,
27	flexibility-endurance, flexibility-speed, skill, strength-skill, flexibility-skill,
28	speed-skill, and skill-endurance. Relative versions of these qualities (per unit bodymass)
29	matter separately in sports where bodymass is constrained (e.g. weight-class sports). (PDF
30	pp. 102-103, printed pp. 91-92.)
31	
32	**Why it works:** Inference: rather than treating strength, speed, endurance, and
33	flexibility as four independent boxes, this model treats them as vertices whose pairwise
34	and triple combinations describe most of the specific fitness qualities that actually
35	appear in sport, with skill/neuromuscular control cutting across all of them. Note: at
36	printed 92 the text itself calls strength-speed and speed-strength "synonymous with the
37	ability to develop great power," not two distinct qualities; the strength-speed vs.
38	speed-strength split already used in
39	[[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]] is attributed there to
40	"some authorities" (printed 20), not to this pyramidal model.
41	
42	**When to apply:** **Inference:** useful as a master vocabulary/reference when precisely
43	naming which quality a given test or exercise targets (e.g. "flexibility-strength" versus
44	plain flexibility), and as a teaching framework (e.g. HHPR 5355) for showing students why
45	"fitness" is not one thing to test or train, but a structured set of specific, combinable
46	qualities. This model treats strength-speed and speed-strength as synonyms (printed 92);
47	for the distinction some authorities draw, see
48	[[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]] (printed 20).
49	
50	**When NOT to apply:** The text itself calls this model "representational or
51	descriptive rather than scientifically analytical" and notes it is complicated by other
52	factors such as quasi-isometric states at very slow speeds (PDF p. 103, printed p. 92);
53	**Inference:** don't treat it as a validated measurement taxonomy with defined tests for
54	each named compound quality — most of these terms (e.g. "flexibility-skill") have no
55	standard test attached in this text.
56	
57	**Example:** **Inference:** describing an athlete's need as "relative strength-speed"
58	(power per unit bodymass) rather than just "power" gives a program design target that is
59	precise about both the force-velocity region and the bodymass constraint, useful for a
60	weight-class or position-limited athlete.

# The S-Factors Pyramidal Model of Fitness (Strength, Speed, Stamina, Suppleness, Skill, Structure, Spirit)

**What it is:** A comprehensive model of fitness built from seven "S-factors": Strength,
Speed, Stamina (systemic or local muscular endurance), Suppleness (flexibility), Skill
(neuromuscular efficiency, including a "Style" sub-quality — an individual's manner of
expressing a skill), Structure (somatotype, size, shape), and Spirit (psychological
preparedness). The model is built in two stages: a triangular base relating strength,
stamina, speed, and suppleness, then a pyramid adding skill/neuromuscular control as the
process that makes all movement possible, with flexibility placed at the center of the
base because range of movement underlies expression of every other quality. From the
pairwise relationships between factors, an extended list of compound fitness qualities is
derived: static/dynamic strength and strength-endurance, strength-speed, speed-strength,
speed-strength endurance, strength-speed endurance, speed, endurance, flexibility-strength,
flexibility-endurance, flexibility-speed, skill, strength-skill, flexibility-skill,
speed-skill, and skill-endurance. Relative versions of these qualities (per unit bodymass)
matter separately in sports where bodymass is constrained (e.g. weight-class sports). (PDF
pp. 102-103, printed pp. 91-92.)

**Why it works:** Inference: rather than treating strength, speed, endurance, and
flexibility as four independent boxes, this model treats them as vertices whose pairwise
and triple combinations describe most of the specific fitness qualities that actually
appear in sport, with skill/neuromuscular control cutting across all of them. Note: at
printed 92 the text itself calls strength-speed and speed-strength "synonymous with the
ability to develop great power," not two distinct qualities; the strength-speed vs.
speed-strength split already used in
[[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]] is attributed there to
"some authorities" (printed 20), not to this pyramidal model.

**When to apply:** **Inference:** useful as a master vocabulary/reference when precisely
naming which quality a given test or exercise targets (e.g. "flexibility-strength" versus
plain flexibility), and as a teaching framework (e.g. HHPR 5355) for showing students why
"fitness" is not one thing to test or train, but a structured set of specific, combinable
qualities. This model treats strength-speed and speed-strength as synonyms (printed 92);
for the distinction some authorities draw, see
[[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]] (printed 20).

**When NOT to apply:** The text itself calls this model "representational or
descriptive rather than scientifically analytical" and notes it is complicated by other
factors such as quasi-isometric states at very slow speeds (PDF p. 103, printed p. 92);
**Inference:** don't treat it as a validated measurement taxonomy with defined tests for
each named compound quality — most of these terms (e.g. "flexibility-skill") have no
standard test attached in this text.

**Example:** **Inference:** describing an athlete's need as "relative strength-speed"
(power per unit bodymass) rather than just "power" gives a program design target that is
precise about both the force-velocity region and the bodymass constraint, useful for a
weight-class or position-limited athlete.

14	# Lactate Does Not "Poison" Muscle or Cause Soreness; "Oxygen Debt" Is an Outdated Concept
15	
16	**What it is:** Two corrections to common misconceptions. (1) Muscle fatigue is not due
17	to "lactic acid poisoning"; lactate formation is accompanied by hydrogen ions that increase
18	acidity and can interfere with contraction and enzyme efficiency, but lactate itself is not
19	the toxin popularly described, and blood lactate returns to normal within about an hour of
20	strenuous interval training — well before delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) typically
21	peaks. The most pronounced soreness actually occurs after prolonged endurance efforts kept
22	below the lactate threshold, so current theory attributes soreness to transient muscle
23	cell or connective tissue damage, not lactic acid. (2) The classic "oxygen debt" concept
24	(the idea that post-exercise heavy breathing "repays" an oxygen deficit incurred during
25	anaerobic work) is now considered outdated; the post-exercise period instead reflects
26	recovery oxygen consumption used to regenerate ATP and CP and restore respiratory, ionic,
27	circulatory, hormonal, and thermal systems to baseline (McArdle, Katch & Katch, 1991). The
28	text says the former "anaerobic threshold" is now referred to as the "blood lactate
29	threshold (or turnpoint) or OBLA (Onset of Blood Lactate Accumulation)" (printed 78). (PDF
30	pp. 87, 89, printed pp. 76, 78.)
31	
32	**Why it works:** Both corrections reflect the same underlying update in exercise
33	physiology: lactate is a normal metabolic byproduct and fuel source, not an anaerobic waste
34	product to be "cleared" or "repaid," and glycolysis runs alongside oxidative metabolism
35	rather than only replacing it when oxygen is absent (also noted in this book: glycolysis
36	dominates during sprinting even though muscles have adequate oxygen).
37	
38	**When to apply:** **Inference:** useful for correcting persistent coaching-room and
39	classroom misconceptions (e.g. in HHPR 5355 teaching) — "lactic acid causes the burn and
40	next-day soreness" and "you're paying back oxygen debt after a sprint" are both outdated
41	framings that this entry can directly correct with citable sources.
42	
43	**When NOT to apply:** **Inference:** correcting the mechanism does not mean lactate is
44	irrelevant to training; the blood lactate threshold (OBLA) remains a legitimate, useful
45	marker for endurance training intensity and athlete conditioning status — only the
46	"lactic acid as toxin/soreness cause" framing and the "oxygen debt" framing are being
47	corrected here, not the practical value of lactate-threshold-based training zones.
48	Inference: the H+/acidosis fatigue mechanism the authors give here (increased acidity
49	"can interfere with the muscle contraction process") is itself contested in modern work
50	(Westerblad, Allen & Lannergren 2002, News Physiol Sci 17:17; Allen, Lamb & Westerblad
51	2008, Physiol Rev 88:287); `proven` here covers only the two named corrections (lactate is
52	not the cause of DOMS; oxygen debt is replaced by recovery oxygen consumption and EPOC),
53	not the H+/acidosis fatigue mechanism.
54	
55	**Example:** **Inference:** an athlete sore two days after a hard endurance session is
56	more likely dealing with muscle/connective tissue microtrauma than residual lactate, which
57	would have cleared within an hour; recovery guidance should be based on that, not on
58	"flushing out lactic acid."
59	
60	**Related:** [[claim--energy-system-contribution-by-sport-table]].
61

# Functional vs. Structural Resistance Training

**What it is:** Two basic categories of resistance training effect: structural training
targets muscle hypertrophy (and some tissue flexibility); functional training targets
performance qualities (static strength, speed-strength, muscular endurance, reactive
ability) through four neural mechanisms: (1) intermuscular coordination — sequencing and
synchronizing action between different muscle groups; (2) intramuscular coordination —
control within one muscle via number encoding (how many fibres are recruited), rate
encoding (firing frequency), and pattern encoding (sequencing of fibre types); (3)
facilitatory/inhibitory reflex processes; (4) motor learning, programming the CNS to
execute a specific task. No training is purely structural; all training is functional to
some degree and may also elicit structural change. (PDF p. 18, printed p. 7.)

**Why it works:** The authors state the sequence ("in the early stages of training or
during stagnation at an advanced level, the functional stages should precede the
structural stages," printed 8) but give no mechanism for it. Inference: force output for a
given movement is the product of both how much contractile tissue exists (structural) and
how effectively the nervous system recruits, times, and sequences that tissue (functional).
Early or stagnation-phase training may get more return from the functional side because
coordination has more room to improve; structural change is slower and more load-dependent.

**When to apply:** The authors state functional stages should precede structural
stages both for beginners and during a plateau at an advanced level (PDF p. 19, printed p.
8, cross-referenced to 1.2 and Ch2). **Inference:** this supports using the split as a
diagnostic lens when an athlete's strength stalls: ask whether the limiter is likely
structural (needs more hypertrophy-phase volume) or functional (needs improved
coordination, rate coding, or motor learning of the specific lift/skill); this diagnostic
framing is this entry's own extension, not stated as a test procedure in the text.

**When NOT to apply:** **Inference:** this is a conceptual split, not a measured
diagnostic; number, rate, and pattern encoding are not directly observable from a force
plate or barbell velocity alone, so inferring which mechanism is limiting a given athlete
is coach judgment, not a test result. The authors' use of "functional training" here
means neural coordination and recruitment specifically (PDF p. 18, printed p. 7);
**Inference:** don't confuse it with the modern commercial-gym use of the same term
(balance boards, unstable surfaces), which is a different, later usage the text does not
address.

**Example:** **Inference:** A lifter whose 1RM is stagnant despite visible muscle gain may be limited by
intermuscular coordination (poor bracing/synchronization under heavy load) rather than by
insufficient muscle; technique and coordination work, not more volume, is the higher-value
fix.

**Related:** [[principle--neuromuscular-stimulation-drives-early-strength-gains]].

# Types of Maximal Strength (CFmax, TFmax, Fmm, Relative Strength)

**What it is:** The authors (citing Zatsiorsky) separate "maximum strength" into a
ladder of distinct maxima, from lowest to highest: training maximum (TFmax, the training
1RM, the heaviest load one can lift without a large emotional/heart-rate spike),
competitive maximum (CFmax, the true 1RM produced under optimal competitive motivation),
and absolute strength (Fmm, "maximum of all maxima," the involuntary ceiling reachable
only under electrical stimulation or a sudden reflex-recruited load, e.g. a sudden drop
or stretch reflex). Relative strength is strength per unit bodymass for a given lift.
Voluntary maxima also rank by contraction type, in order of magnitude: eccentric >
isometric > concentric. (PDF pp. 12-13, printed pp. 1-2.)

**Why it works:** Nervous system inhibition (protective feedback, comparable to a
mechanical governor) normally prevents a muscle from contracting to the point of
structural failure. Competitive arousal and motivation reduce that inhibition further
than routine training effort does, which is why CFmax exceeds TFmax; involuntary or
reflex-driven recruitment removes still more of it, which is why Fmm exceeds CFmax.

**When to apply:** The authors state the competitive maximum, not the daily training
maximum, should set %-based intensity zones for higher-level athletes, because CFmax stays
comparatively stable while TFmax fluctuates day to day (PDF p. 13, printed p. 2).
**Inference:** this ladder is a useful lens for deciding which measured maximum should
anchor programmed intensity for a given athlete. **Eric's baseline:** velocity-based 1RM
estimation (linear-displacement transducer, target mean velocity) is preferred over live
1RM attempts to avoid the fatigue and injury risk of true maxing (`method-baseline.md`,
"Testing and assessment," citing `ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md`; flagged there as
"Inferred (author uncertain — legacy protocol)," and that same Assessment Manual is
separately flagged as likely outdated since it is built around GymAware, not the current
Perch-centered stack). **Inference:** that preference is consistent with this framework's
logic of anchoring intensity to a stable maximum rather than a noisy daily one, though the
baseline document does not itself cite Zatsiorsky's TFmax/CFmax terminology, and Perch is
not itself named in the baseline material as the current 1RM-estimation tool.

**When NOT to apply:** This is a terminology and reasoning framework, not a measured
protocol; Fmm requires electrical stimulation or reflex loading, which the text
calls impractical (PDF p. 12, printed p. 1). **Inference:** none of these four
maxima are named as routinely and directly measured in Baylor's own documented protocols
(`method-baseline.md`), so this should be treated as a mental model for why training-day
and competition-day 1RMs diverge, not as a set of numbers to test for. The text gives the
eccentric > isometric > concentric ordering "as a matter of interest" (printed 2) without
stating it is a fixed ratio; Inference: it likely varies by joint angle, velocity, and
muscle group, though the text does not make that qualification in this passage.

**Example:** **Inference:** An athlete's best training-day squat (TFmax) is consistently lower than
what they hit in a max-out competition or meet (CFmax); programming off the meet number
rather than a re-tested gym max avoids under-loading the athlete for weeks after a strong
competitive performance.

**Related:** [[claim--voluntary-involuntary-strength-reserve-magnitudes]] (the numeric
gaps between these maxima); [[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]]
(a practical field proxy for the same voluntary/involuntary gap).

# Central vs. Peripheral Fatigue, and Low- vs. High-Frequency Fatigue

**What it is:** Fatigue during short-duration strength/power work is split into
**central fatigue** (reduced motivation, impaired spinal nerve transmission, reduced motor
neuron recruitment and firing rate — a CNS-level phenomenon) and **peripheral fatigue**
(failure somewhere in the excitation-contraction chain at the muscle cell itself: motor
end-plate, sarcolemma, T-tubules, sarcoplasmic reticulum, contractile proteins).
Peripheral fatigue further splits into **low-frequency fatigue** (impaired force at <20 Hz
stimulation, from depressed calcium release, with a prolonged recovery period "persisting
for as long as 48 hours," printed 15) and **high-frequency fatigue** (impaired force at
>50 Hz; the text gives no recovery-speed comparison between the two, printed 14-15).
Two distinct purposes are given for reduced central drive during fatigue, on different
pages: for short-term maximal contractions, the reduction in motor-neuron firing rate "may
be beneficial in avoiding electrical failure and facilitating maximal mechanical response"
(printed 15); separately, "muscle wisdom," the CNS's down-regulation of motor neuron
discharge rate during a sustained contraction, has a purpose "believed to ensure that
central neural drive to fatigued skeletal muscle matches that which is needed to generate
the required force," and "may be one mechanism that functions either to decrease or to
postpone central neural fatigue" (printed 16). Exercise-induced ammonia accumulation is
cited as a possible contributor to central fatigue at high intensities/durations. Intensive
CNS activation (max weights, max power, plyometrics) is stated to need at least 48 hours of
recovery if no restorative methods are used. (PDF pp. 24-27, printed pp. 13-16.)

**Why it works:** Inference: fatigue is not a single process with one cause; the
central/peripheral split and the frequency-dependent split reflect genuinely different
physiological bottlenecks (nervous drive vs. contractile-machinery failure vs.
calcium-handling kinetics), which is why they have different time courses.

**When to apply:** The authors state intensive CNS activation (max weights, max power,
plyometrics) needs at least 48 hours of recovery if no restorative methods are used (PDF p.
26, printed p. 15). **Inference:** this supports spacing high-CNS-cost sessions (max
strength, high-velocity work) at least two days apart within a microcycle, and treating
"still feels flat two days after a max-effort day" as plausible central fatigue rather than
assuming poor effort or motivation; this specific practical framing is not stated in the
text.

**When NOT to apply:** **Inference:** this is a mechanistic taxonomy from exercise
physiology, not a monitoring protocol. **Eric's baseline:** modified reactive strength
index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing is the department's chosen daily readiness marker
(`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
`2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`); **Inference:** mRSI is a downstream readiness proxy,
not a direct central/peripheral fatigue assay, so a flat CMJ day should not be
over-attributed to a specific named mechanism (e.g., "low-frequency fatigue") without EMG
or stimulation data — neither source states this equivalence, and this caution is this
entry's own judgment.

**Example:** Inference: a depressed CMJ the day after max squats more likely reflects
residual fatigue than lost strength; retest at 48 hours rather than reacting to a single
depressed value.

**Related:** [[framework--factors-limiting-strength-production]].

# Table 1.1 — Resistance Training Prescription by Goal (Strength, Power, Hypertrophy, Endurance)

**What it is:** A dynamic (non-isometric) resistance-training prescription chart by
goal (PDF p. 22, printed p. 11):

| Variable | Strength | Power | Hypertrophy | Endurance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Load (% 1RM) | 80-100 | 70-100 | 60-80 | 40-60 |
| Reps/set | 1-5 | 1-5 | 8-15 | 25-60 |
| Sets/exercise | 4-7 | 3-5 | 4-8 | 2-4 |
| Rest between sets | 2-6 min | 2-6 min | 2-5 min | 1-2 min |
| Duration/set | 5-10 s | 4-8 s | 20-60 s | 80-150 s |
| Speed/rep (% max) | 60-100 | 90-100 | 60-90 | 6-80 (as printed; probably a misprint for 60-80) |
| Sessions/week | 3-6 | 3-6 | 5-7 | 8-14 |

High-volume, low-resistance work is called an **extensive** method (an
**extensification/accumulation** phase); low-volume, high-intensity work is an
**intensive** method (an **intensification** phase). Early training typically opens with
an extensive phase before progressing to an intensive one; periodization is described as
cyclically alternating these two phase types.

**Why it works:** The author gives no mechanism for the table itself. Inference: each goal
loads the neuromuscular and metabolic systems differently: near-maximal loads at low reps
bias neural recruitment and force capacity (strength); high-velocity submaximal loads bias
rate of force development (power); moderate loads at moderate-to-high volume bias metabolic
and mechanical stress for hypertrophy; light loads at very high reps bias oxidative/
metabolic endurance.

**When to apply:** **Inference:** usable as a first-pass, generic reference when scoping a
new program's load/volume targets by goal, and as shared vocabulary for extensive/intensive
phase naming. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355 already teaches undulating/non-linear
periodization (Parker/Miller/Panariello), waving volume week to week, stated as the
personally preferred model over strict linear progression (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength
and power," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.24-26`). **Inference:** that
undulating model and this text's extensive/intensive phase language describe related but
not identical ideas (wave-to-wave volume change vs. phase-to-phase intensity change); the
baseline material does not cite the book's specific terminology.

**When NOT to apply:** The authors state this chart is "adequate for the average
personal trainer or coach dealing with the average client or lower level athlete" but
incomplete for advanced athletes: it ignores strength-speed, explosive strength,
flexibility-strength, and strength-endurance as separate qualities (PDF p. 21, printed p.
10; the "average personal trainer" quote is PDF p. 22, printed p. 11), and ignores the other
prescription variables covered in
[[heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age]] and later chapters.
**Inference:** do
not use this table as a complete program design tool for a well-trained collegiate
athlete; treat it as a starting reference, not an endpoint.

**Example:** **Inference:** Blocking out approximate set/rep/load ranges for a new hypertrophy-emphasis
mesocycle (60-80% 1RM, 8-15 reps, 4-8 sets) before layering in the athlete-specific
adjustments the text says this table omits.

**Related:** [[heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age]].

# Beginners Respond to Load Alone; Advanced Athletes Need the Full Variable Set

**What it is:** Load, reps, and sets are described as the traditional core variables of a
weight program, but the text lists a much longer set of variables that matter more as
training age rises: the type of strength fitness required, contraction type, movement
speed by phase, acceleration at critical points, rest interval length and type
(active/passive), exercise sequence,
agonist/antagonist and stabilizer/mover strength balance, static/dynamic range of motion,
individual strength deficit, training history, injury history, and level of sports
proficiency. The proficiency factor is called out as especially important: exact
sequencing of strength, strength-speed, and hypertrophy work barely matters in a
beginner's first weeks/months but matters a great deal for an experienced athlete. Loads
as small as 40% of 1RM can measurably strengthen a beginner but do nothing for an elite
athlete. (PDF pp. 22-23, printed pp. 11-12.)

**Why it works:** The author gives no mechanism. Inference: a novice's nervous system and
tissue are both far from their adaptive ceiling, so almost any consistent stimulus produces
a training effect; an advanced athlete has used up most of that low-hanging adaptive room,
so the remaining gains depend on precisely managing the variables that were negligible for
the novice.

**When to apply:** **Inference:** this supports a rule for how much programming detail is
worth the coaching time — spend detailed variable-management effort (sequencing, rest
structure, ROM, asymmetry work) on advanced/experienced athletes, and keep novice
programming simple and consistency-focused. This library's Bompa book makes a related point
from the development-model side ([[periodization--bompa/heuristic--biological-vs-training-age|Biological
vs Chronological vs Training Age]]), though that entry addresses age-grouping and injury
risk rather than this book's programming-variable-complexity angle specifically.

**When NOT to apply:** **Inference:** don't use "they're a beginner" as an excuse to
ignore movement quality, technique, or safety variables; the text's simplification applies
to programming complexity (sequencing, minor load percentages, PDF pp. 22-23, printed pp.
11-12), not to coaching attention on how an exercise is performed — this distinction is
this entry's own reading, not stated explicitly in the text. **Inference:** an older
athlete new to formal training still has a low training age by this logic and should be
treated as a beginner by this rule, not by chronological age; the text does not
draw that chronological-vs-training-age distinction itself in this section.

**Example:** **Inference:** A true freshman gains strength on almost any structured 3x/week program with
straightforward load progression; a fourth-year starter needs exercise sequencing,
recovery structure, and asymmetry correction actively managed to keep progressing.

**Related:** [[framework--resistance-training-prescription-by-goal]].

# Rate of Force (or Tension) Development Is a Separate Limiter from Maximal Force

**What it is:** Sporting performance does not depend simply on the ability to produce
maximum force, because many sporting actions happen too fast to recruit an adequate
number of muscle fibres in the available time. Rate of Force Development (RFD) / Rate of
Tension Development (RTD) — how quickly force rises, not just its ceiling — is named as an
independently important limiter, worth assessing on its own alongside maximal-force
deficits. (PDF p. 21, printed p. 10; cross-referenced to 2.2.1 for more detail.)

**Why it works:** Inference: many athletic actions (sprint ground contact, jump takeoff,
change of direction) last far less time than it takes to reach true maximal voluntary
force. An athlete can have high 1RM strength but a slow force-time curve, and still
underperform in short-duration actions, because the task ends before peak force is reached.
This distinction (peak force vs. rate of rise to a sub-maximal time point) is documented in
modern force-time curve analysis outside this text (e.g. Maffiuletti et al. 2016, "Rate of
force development: physiological and methodological considerations," Eur J Appl Physiol
116:1091-1116), which the text itself does not cite.

**When to apply:** **Eric's baseline:** force-plate metric selection follows the
Output/Driver/Strategy/Fluffy (ODSF) framework, picking 1-2 output metrics, 1-3 driver
metrics (e.g. braking/propulsive force), and 1-3 strategy metrics (e.g. phase durations)

# Compensatory (Acceleration/Action) Training — Using Proprioceptive Feedback to Actively Manage Bar Speed

**What it is:** Free weights (unlike some variable-resistance machines) let the lifter
feel changing leverage through the range of motion via proprioceptive feedback and respond
by voluntarily accelerating or decelerating the bar to raise or lower the force produced.
This is termed Compensatory Acceleration Training (CAT), most obviously used
concentrically, but the text argues it applies just as much eccentrically (muscles
actively resist gravity's acceleration to control the descent) and even isometrically
(the lifter must continuously compensate for fatigue-driven declines in neural drive to
hold a constant position), leading the author to prefer "Compensatory Action Training" as
the fuller name. (PDF p. 32, printed p. 21; Ch 7.1 develops it further.)

**Why it works:** Because force is not fixed by the weight alone (F = ma; a lighter bar
accelerated hard can still produce meaningful force), an athlete who actively drives bar
speed rather than passively moving a fixed load is directly manipulating the training
stimulus at every point in the range of motion, not just at the load's nominal percentage
of 1RM.

**When to apply:** **Inference:** this reads as a conceptual ancestor of today's
velocity-based training (VBT) cueing — "move the bar as fast as possible" instructions on
submaximal sets are a modern implementation of the same idea. **Eric's baseline:** Perch
camera-based velocity-based training is part of the department's current technology stack
(`method-baseline.md`, "Data, technology and reporting," citing
`baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.7`). **Inference:** CAT's proprioceptive-feedback
logic maps onto that existing Perch capability, though neither the book nor the baseline
draws this connection directly. **Inference:** also useful as coaching language for
eccentric-phase control (actively resisting the descent) and isometric holds (actively
maintaining tension); this extension beyond the text's own concentric framing is this
entry's own reading of the authors' eccentric/isometric CAT discussion (PDF p. 32,
printed p. 21).

**When NOT to apply:** **Inference:** this is a technique/cueing concept, not a
load-prescription protocol; it doesn't specify a percentage, velocity target, or rep scheme
on its own in the text. **Inference:** cueing maximal intended acceleration on every rep is
not appropriate for all training goals (e.g., controlled-tempo hypertrophy work
deliberately avoids this); this caveat is not addressed in this section of the text.

**Example:** **Inference:** Coaching "explode the bar up" on a submaximal front squat set is applying
CAT: the athlete voluntarily increases bar acceleration beyond what the load alone would
produce, raising the true training force above the load's nominal value.

**Related:** [[principle--equal-force-different-loading-methods]].

# The Force-Velocity Relationship, and Why Strength Doesn't Guarantee Speed

**What it is:** Hill's hyperbolic force-velocity curve: velocity of contraction is
inversely related to load; large force cannot be produced at very high velocities under
constant conditions; heavy strength training shifts the curve upward, particularly in
beginners (raising force at all velocities, called training for "strength-speed"); light,
high-velocity training shifts the curve's velocity maximum rightward (called training for
"speed-strength"). Because power = force x velocity, both shifts raise power, just at
different points on the curve. Zatsiorsky (1995) reports "there is no correlation between
maximal velocity and maximal strength" (printed 20); the ability to generate maximum
strength and to produce high speed are described as different motor abilities. Inference:
this specific claim is contested by modern data (Wisloff et al. 2004, Br J Sports Med
38:285, squat 1RM vs. 10 m sprint time, r ~0.94; Seitz et al. 2014, Sports Med, strength
gains transferring to sprint performance). (PDF pp. 30-31, printed pp. 19-20; Zatsiorsky &
Matveev 1964, Komi 1979, Zatsiorsky 1995.)

**Why it works:** The Hill curve, "although this relationship originally was derived for
isolated muscle, ... has been confirmed for actual sporting movement" (printed 19). Beyond
that author's statement, the rest is Inference: the F-V relationship reflects the
cross-bridge cycling and motor unit recruitment limits of muscle contraction, and is the
conceptual ancestor of the force-velocity profiling methods (Samozino, Morin, and others)
used in modern sprint and jump testing; the book does not itself draw that connection to
modern profiling.

**When to apply:** **Inference:** justifies programming that targets a specific region of
the force-velocity spectrum rather than assuming "more strength" automatically transfers to
speed: heavy-load, low-velocity work develops the force end; light-load, high-velocity
(including ballistic/plyometric) work develops the velocity end. **Inference:** usable as
the conceptual basis for choosing between a strength-speed or speed-strength emphasis block
for an athlete whose limiter has been identified (e.g., via jump testing or sprint
force-velocity profiling); this specific screening application is not stated in the text.

**When NOT to apply:** **Inference:** don't treat "no correlation between max strength and
max velocity" (PDF p. 31, printed p. 20) as license to ignore strength training for a
speed-limited athlete; a certain strength floor is plausibly still necessary before
speed-specific training pays off. **Eric's baseline:** the Vermeil hierarchy of athletic
development (work capacity, then strength, then power, then speed, then sport skill) is
repeatedly described as the department's programming "compass" (`method-baseline.md`,
"Strength and power," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.9-10,18-19`).
**Inference:** that sequencing is broadly consistent with treating a strength floor as a
prerequisite, though neither this text's cited section nor the baseline states the two
frameworks are equivalent. The text itself flags the classic hyperbolic F-V curve as not
universally accurate: research on the lumbar erector spinae shows a "yielding" drop in
force during constant-velocity eccentric stretching that the standard curve doesn't predict
(Sutarno & McGill, 1995; PDF p. 30, printed p. 19) — the model is a strong generalization,
not a universal law for every muscle group.

**Example:** **Inference:** Two athletes with equal back squat 1RM (similar max force) can have very
different unloaded sprint speeds; that gap is F-V curve position, not raw strength, and
argues for velocity-end training (sprint work, light-load ballistics) rather than more
heavy squatting to close it.

**Related:** [[principle--torque-optimization-in-lifting-technique]],
[[principle--equal-force-different-loading-methods]].

# Soviet Sport-School Guideline Ages by Sport (Start, Specialize, Peak)

**What it is:** A per-sport table (Table 1.2) of recommended ages to begin a sport,
begin specialization, and expect high performance, drawn from the Soviet sports-school
system. Examples: basketball 7-8 / 10-12 / 20-25; gymnastics (women) 4-5 / 10-11 / 14-18;
gymnastics (men) 5-6 / 12-14 / 18-24; swimming 3-7 / 10-12 / 16-18; track-and-field 6-7 /
13-14 / 18-23; weightlifting 10-11 / 17-18 / 21-28; wrestling 10-11 / 15-16 / 24-28 (17
sports listed in total). Early, intense specialization is explicitly discouraged in
strength and endurance sports for children; the average age of Soviet Olympians in the
era cited was about 24, with fewer than 10% under age 20. (PDF pp. 35-36, printed pp.
24-25.)

**Why it works:** **Inference:** the likely underlying rationale matches this library's
existing long-term athletic development material — early specialization in
strength/endurance sports produces faster short-term progress but a lower ultimate ceiling
and more attrition, because the young athlete has not built the broad physical base
specialization later draws on. The text does not itself restate this mechanism in this
passage; it presents the table and the age-of-Olympians statistic as its supporting
evidence (PDF p. 36, printed p. 25). The text does note one exception: "many Russian
experts" hold that early specialization is possible in sports emphasizing coordination,
agility, flexibility, or speed (e.g. gymnastics), because of the pre-adolescent's
particular ability in those respects; strength and endurance sports are discouraged for
youngsters specifically (printed 25).

break it out by individual sport; this convergence is this entry's own comparison, not
stated in either source.

not a modern, population-representative dataset; individual biological maturation varies
(see [[periodization--bompa/heuristic--biological-vs-training-age|Biological vs Training
Age]]), and American collegiate sport pathways (e.g. football, not listed in Table 1.2 at
all) do not map cleanly onto these Soviet age bands. Treat the specific ages as
illustrative, not prescriptive, for a Baylor Athletics context; this caution is this
entry's own judgment.

**Example:** **Inference:** The table's general caution against early strength/endurance specialization
supports keeping a young multi-sport athlete on broad physical preparation rather than

# Strength Training Adapts Along (at Least) Ten Independent, Narrow Dimensions

**What it is:** Strength gains transfer narrowly, not generally, across at least ten
independent dimensions: type of muscle contraction, movement pattern, region/range of
movement, velocity of movement, force of contraction, muscle fibre recruitment,
metabolism, biochemical adaptation, flexibility, and fatigue. Training that improves one
dimension often produces little or no improvement on the others, even when the same
muscle groups are involved. Specificity is explicitly distinguished from simulation:
"simulation of a sporting movement with small added resistance over the full range of
movement or with larger resistance over a restricted part of the movement range may be
appropriate at certain stages of training," but "simulation of any movement with
significant resistance is inadvisable since it can confuse the neuromuscular programmes"
(printed 27), because of changes in center of gravity, moment of inertia, and mechanical
stiffness introduced by the resistance. (PDF pp. 38-39, printed pp. 27-28.)

**Why it works:** Strength adaptation is produced and expressed by the nervous and
muscular systems together (see
[[principle--neuromuscular-stimulation-drives-early-strength-gains]]); the specific
demands (velocity, joint angle, contraction type, metabolic pathway) shape which
recruitment patterns, fibre types, and biochemical pathways are trained, so a change in
any one of those parameters can produce a materially different, largely non-transferable
adaptation. Inference: the book's own ten-dimension taxonomy and the "little or no
improvement on the others" claim are the authors' own framework, not independently
established as stated; see
[[periodization--bompa/principle--specificity-of-adaptation]] for this library's in-vault
discussion of specificity.

**When to apply:** **Inference:** usable as a master reasoning check before assuming an
exercise "transfers" to a sport skill: ask which of the ten dimensions the exercise
actually matches, not just whether it uses similar muscles. **Eric's baseline:** the
Principle of Dynamic Correspondence (Verkhoshansky) — matching amplitude/direction of
movement, region of force production, dynamics of effort, rate/timing of force production,
and regime of muscular work to the sport skill — governs whether an exercise transfers, and
is taught in HHPR 5355 (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing
`01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.14`, `week1-lecture.md p.34`). **Inference:**
Dynamic Correspondence (this book's Ch4.3, not yet ingested) is plausibly the applied
extension of this same ten-dimension specificity logic to exercise selection, though this
chapter does not itself state that link.

**When NOT to apply:** **Inference:** don't use "specificity" as an argument against any
general preparation work; this book's own 1.1 material and this library's Bompa
multilateral/LTAD entries support building a general base before narrowing to sport-specific
work. This principle governs which dimensions transfer, not whether general work has value
at an earlier training age; that distinction is this entry's own reading, not stated as
such in this passage of the text.

**Example:** **Inference:** Heavy squat strength does not automatically transfer to high-velocity sprint
force production (different point on the velocity dimension) even though both use similar
musculature; each needs its own specific training exposure.

**Related:** [[claim--velocity-and-contraction-specificity-asymmetric-transfer]],
[[claim--bilateral-deficit-and-limb-training-specificity]],
[[periodization--bompa/principle--specificity-of-adaptation]].

# Work Capacity, Fitness, and Preparedness Are Three Different Things

**What it is:** Verkhoshansky (citing Zatsiorsky) defines three related but distinct
terms. Work capacity is the general ability of the body to produce work of different
intensity and duration using its energy systems. Fitness is the specific ability to use
that work capacity to execute a given task efficiently and safely; it is a slow-changing
state that does not vary meaningfully over a period of days. Preparedness is not stable:
it is the resultant, at any given instant, of the interaction between the slow-changing
fitness component and the fast-changing, opposing effect of exercise-induced fatigue.
"Instantaneous preparedness" can be pushed down by transient factors (mental state,
sickness, fatigue, sleepiness) without any change in underlying fitness. (PDF pp. 43-44,
printed pp. 32-33; developed further at 1.16.3.)

**Why it works:** Separating a slow, structural capacity (fitness) from a fast,
state-dependent expression of it (preparedness) explains why an athlete's fitness can be
objectively unchanged from one day to the next while their measured or perceived output
still swings substantially, because the fatigue component is riding on top of a stable
base.

**When to apply:** **Eric's baseline:** preparedness (the athlete's underlying physical
capability, built over a long period) is explicitly distinguished from readiness
(day-to-day fluctuation) in the department's own testing philosophy, with both tracked
because they answer different questions (`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment,"
citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.7`). **Inference:** that distinction maps
closely onto this framework's fitness/preparedness split (fitness ~ the baseline's
"preparedness," Verkhoshansky's "preparedness" ~ the baseline's "readiness"), though the
two sources use the words differently and neither cites the other; a reader moving between
them should track the underlying concept, not the label.

**When NOT to apply:** **Inference:** the terminology mismatch matters — do not assume
"preparedness" means the same thing in both sources without checking which sense is
meant, since Verkhoshansky's "preparedness" is the department's "readiness," not its
"preparedness." This entry's own definitions above use Verkhoshansky's terms throughout.

**Example:** **Inference:** an athlete whose long-term strength and conditioning markers
(fitness/base preparedness) have been stable for weeks can still show a depressed CMJ
reading (Verkhoshansky's "instantaneous preparedness," the baseline's "readiness") after
poor sleep or travel, without any real loss of underlying capacity.

**Related:** [[framework--central-vs-peripheral-fatigue-mechanisms]].

# Structural and Functional Determinants of Strength

**What it is:** The authors list the factors that determine how much strength a
muscle group can produce. Structural factors: cross-sectional area of the muscle, density
of fibres per unit cross-section, and mechanical leverage efficiency across the joint.
Functional (neural) factors: number of fibres contracting simultaneously, rate of fibre
contraction, efficiency of firing synchronization, nerve conduction velocity, degree of
inhibition of non-contributing fibres, proportion of large-diameter (fast-twitch) fibres
active, efficiency of cooperation between fibre types, efficiency of stretch reflexes,
excitation threshold of the nerve fibres, and initial muscle length before contraction.
Maximum strength is produced at an optimum, not a maximum, frequency of nerve firing
(Vredensky, via Vorobyev 1978), and that optimal frequency itself shifts with fatigue
level (Kernell & Monster, 1982). Synchronization of motor unit firing across fibres does
not appear to meaningfully increase the rate of strength production; sequencing
(efficient timing) may matter more than simultaneity, especially where stored elastic
energy must be released at the right moment (Miller et al., 1981). (PDF pp. 44-45,
printed pp. 33-34.)

**Why it works:** This is a fuller inventory of why two athletes with the same
cross-sectional muscle area can produce very different force: most of the list is neural
(recruitment, timing, inhibition, reflex efficiency), consistent with this chapter's
overall theme that strength is a neuromuscular, not purely structural, phenomenon.

**When to apply:** **Inference:** useful as a longer checklist than
[[framework--functional-vs-structural-resistance-training]] when explaining to students
or staff (e.g. in HHPR 5355) why hypertrophy alone does not fully predict strength, and
for generating hypotheses about why an athlete with good muscle mass underperforms on
force output (check firing rate, synchronization, initial muscle length/joint angle,
rather than assuming a training-volume problem).

**When NOT to apply:** The authors note more research is needed before drawing a
firm conclusion about strength gains from increased motor-unit synchronization (PDF p.
45, printed p. 34); **Inference:** do not treat "improve synchronization" as an
established, targetable training goal on its own — none of these functional factors
listed have a stated field-testable metric in this section.

**Example:** **Inference:** two athletes with similar squat cross-sectional muscle
estimates (e.g. via anthropometrics) but different 1RM outputs are most likely differing
on the functional/neural list (recruitment, firing rate, inhibition), not on structural
factors alone.

**Related:** [[framework--functional-vs-structural-resistance-training]],
[[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]].

# Collagenous Tissue's Four-Region Loading Curve, and Why Loading Rate Changes What Fails First

**What it is:** Collagenous tissue (e.g. the ACL, studied by Frankel & Nordin 1980)
loaded to failure shows four regions: Region I, the "toe region," where the crimped
tissue straightens with little force and mild stretching here produces no long-term
flexibility change; Region II, a near-linear region where fibres are fully uncrimped and
parallel; Region III, where sequential microfailure of overstretched fibres begins; Region
IV, complete failure. Loading rate changes the outcome: increasing loading rate roughly
fourfold raised knee ligament failure load by almost 50% (Kennedy et al., 1976), and which
structure fails first flips with rate — at slow loading rates the ligament's bony
insertion is the weakest link, while at fast loading rates the ligament itself is the
weakest link (bone's strength rises faster with rate than the ligament's). Healthy tendon's
tensile strength can be more than twice that of its associated muscle, which is why
ruptures are more common in muscle than tendon. (PDF pp. 54-56, printed pp. 43-45.)

**Why it works:** Collagen is viscoelastic: it behaves more elastically under rapid
loading and more plastically (creeping, deforming) under slow, sustained loading, so both
the loading speed and the tissue's own rate-dependent stiffness change determine where in
the body an excessive load actually causes failure.

**When to apply:** **Inference:** relevant background for understanding why static
stretching held gently (Region I) does not meaningfully change tissue length or
flexibility over time, and why ballistic or rapid loading, once past Region II, carries
real microfailure risk; also relevant context for why the pattern of injury (bone
avulsion vs. mid-ligament tear vs. muscle strain) can differ by the speed of the loading
event, which matters for how Athletic Medicine and Applied Performance jointly interpret
an injury mechanism.

**When NOT to apply:** **Inference:** this is basic tissue mechanics from cited
1970s-1980s cadaveric/animal ligament research, not a live-tissue, in-vivo human athlete
dataset; do not use the specific numbers (50% failure-load increase, the fourfold rate
figure) as applicable outside the original knee-ligament loading-rate study (Kennedy 1976,
printed 44); only the strain curve (Fig 1.21) is specifically ACL.
This is background science, not a clinical decision rule, and should not substitute for
Athletic Medicine's own injury assessment framework.

**Example:** **Inference:** a sudden high-rate valgus load to the knee is more likely to
produce mid-ligament ACL failure, while a slower, sustained load is more likely to fail at
the bony insertion first; this pattern helps explain, but does not replace, imaging and
clinical exam in determining actual injury location.

**Related:** [[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]],
[[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]].

# The Muscle Model: Series Elastic Component (SEC) vs. Parallel Elastic Component (PEC)

**What it is:** A mechanical model of muscle (Levin & Wyman, 1927) treats it as a
contractile component in series with a Series Elastic Component (SEC: tendon,
cross-bridges, myofilaments, titin, Z-discs) and in parallel with a Parallel Elastic
Component (PEC: sarcolemma, rest-state cross-bridging, surrounding sheaths). The PEC
carries the force of a relaxed muscle stretched beyond resting length, and stores little
usable energy; the SEC is tensioned by an actively contracting muscle resisting a rapid
stretch, and stores considerable elastic energy — this is the mechanism plyometric/shock
training exploits. Slow-twitch (ST) dominant muscle shows smaller mechanical strain when
stretched while contracted but has a stiffer, more elastic SEC than fast-twitch
(FT)-dominant muscle, largely due to higher collagen concentration in slow muscle. The book
gives conflicting statements on which fibre type stores more elastic energy overall:
printed 41 states "the stored elastic energy is greater in FT fibres" (Komi, 1984), while
printed 46 states "a slow muscle can store relatively more elastic energy in its
collagenous tissue than fast muscle." Both are recorded here rather than harmonized.
Static, relaxed, and passive stretching mainly load the PEC; "tense ballistic and active
stretching affects predominantly the SEC," while PNF techniques "appear to be able to
stretch and strengthen both the SEC and the PEC" (printed 41-42). (PDF pp. 51-53, 57;
printed pp. 40-42, 46.)

**Why it works:** Inference: knowing which component (PEC or SEC) is under tension in a
given stretch or contraction explains why static/passive and active/PNF stretching target
different tissue; the book conflicts on which fibre type stores more elastic energy
(printed 41 vs. 46), so no single fibre-type/component pairing can be asserted as the
mechanism.

**When to apply:** **Inference:** useful for explaining why plyometric/reactive-strength
training targets the SEC specifically (rapid stretch under active contraction) rather than
simple static flexibility work (which mostly loads the PEC), and for choosing PNF-style
active stretching when the goal is to influence both components rather than the PEC alone.

**When NOT to apply:** **Inference:** the anatomical location of SEC/PEC elements is
explicitly stated as not precisely identified (PDF p. 52, printed p. 41); treat this as a
functional/mechanical model for reasoning about elastic energy, not a literal anatomical
map to test or measure directly in an athlete.

**Example:** Inference: by the authors' own account, slow postural muscle needs longer
stretching to meaningfully change its flexibility than fast muscle does (printed 41), which
supports muscle-specific rather than uniform flexibility prescription; this is distinct
from, and does not depend on, the unresolved FT-vs-ST elastic-energy-storage conflict
above.

**Related:** [[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]],
[[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]].
