# Precise Muscle-Action Terminology: Why "Isotonic" and "Isokinetic" Are Usually Wrong

**What it is:** The authors argue most everyday strength-training terms are
technically imprecise. Concentric: proximal and distal muscle attachments move toward one
another. Eccentric: they move apart (not literally a "contraction," despite the common
name — the muscle is returning toward resting length under load). Isometric: attachments
don't move relative to each other (joint angle constant); more accurately called "static."
"Isotonic" (constant tension) is argued to be almost never actually true during real joint
movement, since tension changes with acceleration, deceleration, and reflex activation
throughout a range; European and Russian scientists prefer "auxotonic" (changing tension
and length) or "allodynamic" instead. "Isokinetic" (constant velocity) is also argued to
be physically impossible over a full range, since starting from and returning to rest
requires acceleration; isokinetic devices are more accurately "quasi-isokinetic," and
isokinetic-machine torque output is typically much lower than isometric torque at the same
joint angle. "Quasi-isometric" action is defined separately: the slow, near-static muscle
action seen in heavy, near-maximal resistance training performed anywhere across a joint's
range (not fixed at one angle like true isometrics), relevant to maximal strength,
hypertrophy, and active flexibility training rather than power or speed. (PDF pp. 60-64,
printed pp. 49-53.)

**Why it works:** Real joint movement always involves changing acceleration
(Newton's laws), so any term implying a truly constant mechanical variable throughout a
full range is describing an idealization, not the actual muscle physics; the more precise
terms track what is actually held constant and where.

**When to apply:** **Inference:** relevant when interpreting or reporting isokinetic
dynamometer data (if used by Athletic Medicine or research collaborators): understand that
the constant-velocity claim applies only to the device's controlled range, not to the
underlying muscle action, and that isokinetic torque values are not directly comparable to
isometric (e.g. IMTP) values at the same joint angle. Also useful coaching-language
precision: heavy squat/bench-style lifting performed slowly is "quasi-isometric," a
distinct quality from true fixed-angle isometrics like the IMTP.

**When NOT to apply:** **Inference:** this is a terminology-precision argument, not a
claim that isokinetic or isotonic training methods are ineffective; the critique is about
what the words accurately describe, not about training value. Don't over-correct common
usage in casual coaching communication where the imprecise terms are well understood by
convention.

**Example:** **Inference:** describing an IMTP as "isometric" (fixed joint angle) versus
a slow, heavy back squat as "quasi-isometric" (near-static but occurring across a range)
keeps clear which type of force-plate or barbell data is actually comparable to which.

**Related:** [[principle--triphasic-nature-of-muscle-action]].

# All Dynamic Movement Is Triphasic: Isometric, Then Concentric/Eccentric, Then Isometric Again

**What it is:** Classifying muscle action as simply "static" (isometric) or "dynamic"
(concentric/eccentric) is described as an oversimplification. Every dynamic action must
begin from an isometric phase (the muscle must first develop enough tension to
counterbalance the load before any movement starts: concentric if tension exceeds the
load, eccentric if it doesn't), and every movement ends in another isometric phase before
reversing or stopping, because Newton's laws require the system to momentarily come to
rest at a direction change. In ballistic/ fast movement, the transition isometric phase is
very brief; in slow maximal efforts (e.g. a powerlifting squat or bench), it can be much
longer. The brief isometric phase in a plyometric movement is specifically termed
"explosive isometric" action and is central to speed-strength training and movements like
the weightlifting jerk, shot put, and high jump. Movement termination/reversal can also
involve any combination of agonist eccentric or isometric action, antagonist concentric or
isometric action, stabilizer action at the joint or nearby joints, and passive connective-
tissue damping — not simply "antagonist opposes agonist" as popular descriptions suggest.
(PDF pp. 65-66, printed pp. 54-55.)

**Why it works:** This follows directly from Newtonian mechanics (a moving system must
have zero velocity at the instant it reverses direction) combined with the physiological
fact that muscle tension must build before it can move a load; the "explosive isometric"
phase is the same brief coupling window discussed in
[[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]], described here from the
whole-joint-action perspective rather than the cross-bridge perspective.

**When to apply:** **Inference:** reinforces that "isometric strength" is not a separate,
niche quality but a phase present in every dynamic lift and sprint/jump action, which
supports including isometric testing (IMTP) and isometric-emphasis training as directly
relevant to dynamic performance, not a side quality. Also a caution for kinesiology
teaching (e.g. HHPR 5355): movement termination is not simply "antagonist stops agonist";
several structures can share that role, so a simplistic agonist/antagonist explanation for
a given movement's braking phase may be incomplete.

**When NOT to apply:** The text itself notes inappropriate antagonist activation
opposing a strongly contracting agonist is a recognized injury mechanism (e.g. hamstrings
rupturing when they fire to oppose the quadriceps during sprinting or kicking, PDF p. 60,
printed p. 49); **Inference:** this triphasic framework describes normal, coordinated
movement termination, and should not be conflated with that pathological
premature-antagonist-activation injury pattern, which is a distinct, unwanted phenomenon
rather than part of the normal triphasic sequence.

**Example:** **Inference:** a sprinter's ground-contact phase is not purely
"eccentric-then-concentric"; it necessarily includes the brief isometric coupling phase
this principle describes, which is the same window where the reactive-strength/elastic
mechanism in [[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]] operates.

**Related:** [[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]],
[[framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology]].

# Classic Energy-System Percentage Tables by Sport (Fox & Mathews, 1974) — Football Listed at ~90% Phosphagen

**What it is:** The authors reproduce Fox & Mathews' (1974) classic tables (Table 1.4)
estimating the percentage contribution of the short-term (phosphagen/ATP-CP), intermediate
(non-oxidative glycolytic), and long-term (oxidative/aerobic) energy systems to different
training modes and sports. American football is listed at 90% short-term, 10%
intermediate, 0% long-term — among the most phosphagen-dominant sports in the table,
comparable to golf (95/5/0) and volleyball (90/10/0), and far more phosphagen-dominant
than field hockey or soccer half-backs (60/20/20). The authors themselves caution that
"figures for longer duration events such as the 1500m run have been modified by other
researchers and their accuracy needs to be re-examined," that "the highly determinate
nature of this whole scheme, compiled several decades ago, has been questioned more
recently," and that it should not be used casually because it disguises moment-to-moment
metabolic demand shifts within a single sport (printed 81). (PDF pp. 91-92, printed pp.
80-81.)

**Why it works:** The authors state these figures "reflect the average contributions made
by three concurrently operating metabolic systems ... for an average athlete," which
"disguises the fact ... that the metabolic demands often differ from instant to instant
during every type of activity taking place in each sport" (printed 81). Inference: for
football specifically, actual play consists of short high-intensity bursts (plays)
separated by long rest (huddles, substitutions), so an average figure can obscure the real
repeated-sprint, phosphagen-dominant-per-play structure while also underweighting the role
of aerobic recovery between bursts; the text does not itself apply this reasoning to
football.

**When to apply:** **Eric's baseline:** the department's stated conditioning priority for
football is alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp and game demands, with
glycolytic conditioning treated as a "worst case scenario" absorbed incidentally rather
than programmed as a primary target (`method-baseline.md`, "Conditioning and energy
systems," citing `class-4-2026.md pp.34, 39`); the baseline also states the aerobic
system's main value for speed-power athletes is inter-effort recovery (regenerating ATP
between bouts), not distance capacity (citing `2026-02-05-hp5355-class3-transcript.md
p.9`). **Inference:** this table's 90/10/0 split for football (near-zero credited to the
long-term/aerobic system) looks, at first read, to be in tension with the baseline's
explicit inclusion of aerobic capacity as a Goal-1 priority for football — but the tension
likely resolves once "aerobic system" is understood functionally: the baseline treats
aerobic fitness as enabling faster ATP/phosphagen regeneration between the very
phosphagen-dominant plays this table describes, not as a source of in-play energy. Read
together, not as contradictory: this table describes what fuels a single play; the
baseline describes what determines how well that fuel regenerates for the next one.

**When NOT to apply:** The authors' own caution applies directly here: **Inference:** do
not use the 90/10/0 football figure as a precise or current number; it is a decades-old
average estimate for the sport as a whole, not a modern, position-specific or play-by-play
breakdown. The text itself states that "the highly determinate nature of this whole scheme,
compiled several decades ago, has been questioned more recently" and that figures for
longer events "have been modified by other researchers" (printed 81). This entry is rated
`contested` beyond that self-flagged caution because modern measurement puts the aerobic
contribution far higher, and earlier in an effort, than these 1970s tables allow for (e.g.
Gastin, 2001, Sports Med 31:725-741).

**Example:** **Inference:** a single football play (a few seconds of maximal effort)
draws almost entirely on the phosphagen system, consistent with the table; but the
athlete's ability to repeat that near-maximal output play after play, series after series,
depends heavily on aerobic capacity for recovery between plays — the quality the baseline
prioritizes.

**Related:** None in this ingest yet; candidate future link to a conditioning synthesis
note once Phase 4 of the Flint project reaches conditioning and energy systems.

# Lactate Does Not "Poison" Muscle or Cause Soreness; "Oxygen Debt" Is an Outdated Concept

**What it is:** Two corrections to common misconceptions. (1) Muscle fatigue is not due
to "lactic acid poisoning"; lactate formation is accompanied by hydrogen ions that increase
acidity and can interfere with contraction and enzyme efficiency, but lactate itself is not
the toxin popularly described, and blood lactate returns to normal within about an hour of
strenuous interval training — well before delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) typically
peaks. The most pronounced soreness actually occurs after prolonged endurance efforts kept
below the lactate threshold, so current theory attributes soreness to transient muscle
cell or connective tissue damage, not lactic acid. (2) The classic "oxygen debt" concept
(the idea that post-exercise heavy breathing "repays" an oxygen deficit incurred during
anaerobic work) is now considered outdated; the post-exercise period instead reflects
recovery oxygen consumption used to regenerate ATP and CP and restore respiratory, ionic,
circulatory, hormonal, and thermal systems to baseline (McArdle, Katch & Katch, 1991). The
text says the former "anaerobic threshold" is now referred to as the "blood lactate
threshold (or turnpoint) or OBLA (Onset of Blood Lactate Accumulation)" (printed 78). (PDF
pp. 87, 89, printed pp. 76, 78.)

**Why it works:** Both corrections reflect the same underlying update in exercise
physiology: lactate is a normal metabolic byproduct and fuel source, not an anaerobic waste
product to be "cleared" or "repaid," and glycolysis runs alongside oxidative metabolism
rather than only replacing it when oxygen is absent (also noted in this book: glycolysis
dominates during sprinting even though muscles have adequate oxygen).

**When to apply:** **Inference:** useful for correcting persistent coaching-room and
classroom misconceptions (e.g. in HHPR 5355 teaching) — "lactic acid causes the burn and
next-day soreness" and "you're paying back oxygen debt after a sprint" are both outdated
framings that this entry can directly correct with citable sources.

**When NOT to apply:** **Inference:** correcting the mechanism does not mean lactate is
irrelevant to training; the blood lactate threshold (OBLA) remains a legitimate, useful
marker for endurance training intensity and athlete conditioning status — only the
"lactic acid as toxin/soreness cause" framing and the "oxygen debt" framing are being
corrected here, not the practical value of lactate-threshold-based training zones.
Inference: the H+/acidosis fatigue mechanism the authors give here (increased acidity
"can interfere with the muscle contraction process") is itself contested in modern work
(Westerblad, Allen & Lannergren 2002, News Physiol Sci 17:17; Allen, Lamb & Westerblad
2008, Physiol Rev 88:287); `proven` here covers only the two named corrections (lactate is
not the cause of DOMS; oxygen debt is replaced by recovery oxygen consumption and EPOC),
not the H+/acidosis fatigue mechanism.

**Example:** **Inference:** an athlete sore two days after a hard endurance session is
more likely dealing with muscle/connective tissue microtrauma than residual lactate, which
would have cleared within an hour; recovery guidance should be based on that, not on
"flushing out lactic acid."

**Related:** [[claim--energy-system-contribution-by-sport-table]].

# The S-Factors Pyramidal Model of Fitness (Strength, Speed, Stamina, Suppleness, Skill, Structure, Spirit)

**What it is:** A comprehensive model of fitness built from seven "S-factors": Strength,
Speed, Stamina (systemic or local muscular endurance), Suppleness (flexibility), Skill
(neuromuscular efficiency, including a "Style" sub-quality — an individual's manner of
expressing a skill), Structure (somatotype, size, shape), and Spirit (psychological
preparedness). The model is built in two stages: a triangular base relating strength,
stamina, speed, and suppleness, then a pyramid adding skill/neuromuscular control as the
process that makes all movement possible, with flexibility placed at the center of the
base because range of movement underlies expression of every other quality. From the
pairwise relationships between factors, an extended list of compound fitness qualities is
derived: static/dynamic strength and strength-endurance, strength-speed, speed-strength,
speed-strength endurance, strength-speed endurance, speed, endurance, flexibility-strength,
flexibility-endurance, flexibility-speed, skill, strength-skill, flexibility-skill,
speed-skill, and skill-endurance. Relative versions of these qualities (per unit bodymass)
matter separately in sports where bodymass is constrained (e.g. weight-class sports). (PDF
pp. 102-103, printed pp. 91-92.)

**Why it works:** Inference: rather than treating strength, speed, endurance, and
flexibility as four independent boxes, this model treats them as vertices whose pairwise
and triple combinations describe most of the specific fitness qualities that actually
appear in sport, with skill/neuromuscular control cutting across all of them. Note: at
printed 92 the text itself calls strength-speed and speed-strength "synonymous with the
ability to develop great power," not two distinct qualities; the strength-speed vs.
speed-strength split already used in
[[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]] is attributed there to
"some authorities" (printed 20), not to this pyramidal model.

**When to apply:** **Inference:** useful as a master vocabulary/reference when precisely
naming which quality a given test or exercise targets (e.g. "flexibility-strength" versus
plain flexibility), and as a teaching framework (e.g. HHPR 5355) for showing students why
"fitness" is not one thing to test or train, but a structured set of specific, combinable
qualities. This model treats strength-speed and speed-strength as synonyms (printed 92);
for the distinction some authorities draw, see
[[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]] (printed 20).

**When NOT to apply:** The text itself calls this model "representational or
descriptive rather than scientifically analytical" and notes it is complicated by other
factors such as quasi-isometric states at very slow speeds (PDF p. 103, printed p. 92);
**Inference:** don't treat it as a validated measurement taxonomy with defined tests for
each named compound quality — most of these terms (e.g. "flexibility-skill") have no
standard test attached in this text.

**Example:** **Inference:** describing an athlete's need as "relative strength-speed"
(power per unit bodymass) rather than just "power" gives a program design target that is
precise about both the force-velocity region and the bodymass constraint, useful for a
weight-class or position-limited athlete.

**Related:** [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]],
[[framework--work-capacity-fitness-preparedness]].

14	# Functional vs. Structural Resistance Training
15	
16	**What it is** — Two basic categories of resistance training effect: structural training
17	targets muscle hypertrophy (and some tissue flexibility); functional training targets
18	performance qualities (static strength, speed-strength, muscular endurance, reactive
19	ability) through four neural mechanisms: (1) intermuscular coordination, sequencing and
20	synchronizing action between different muscle groups; (2) intramuscular coordination,
21	control within one muscle via number encoding (how many fibres are recruited), rate
22	encoding (firing frequency), and pattern encoding (sequencing of fibre types); (3)
23	facilitatory/inhibitory reflex processes; (4) motor learning, programming the CNS to
24	execute a specific task. No training is purely structural; all training is functional to
25	some degree and may also elicit structural change. (PDF p. 18, printed p. 7.)
26	
27	**Why it works** — The authors state the sequence ("in the early stages of training or
28	during stagnation at an advanced level, the functional stages should precede the
29	structural stages," printed 8) but give no mechanism for it. Inference: force output for a
30	given movement is the product of both how much contractile tissue exists (structural) and
31	how effectively the nervous system recruits, times, and sequences that tissue (functional).
32	Early or stagnation-phase training may get more return from the functional side because
33	coordination has more room to improve; structural change is slower and more load-dependent.
34	
35	**When to apply** — The authors state functional stages should precede structural
36	stages both for beginners and during a plateau at an advanced level (PDF p. 19, printed p.
37	8, cross-referenced to 1.2 and Ch2). **Inference:** this supports using the split as a
38	diagnostic lens when an athlete's strength stalls: ask whether the limiter is likely
39	structural (needs more hypertrophy-phase volume) or functional (needs improved
40	coordination, rate coding, or motor learning of the specific lift/skill); this diagnostic
41	framing is this entry's own extension, not stated as a test procedure in the text.
42	
43	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a conceptual split, not a measured
44	diagnostic; number, rate, and pattern encoding are not directly observable from a force
45	plate or barbell velocity alone, so inferring which mechanism is limiting a given athlete
46	is coach judgment, not a test result. The authors' use of "functional training" here
47	means neural coordination and recruitment specifically (PDF p. 18, printed p. 7);
48	**Inference:** don't confuse it with the modern commercial-gym use of the same term
49	(balance boards, unstable surfaces), which is a different, later usage the text does not
50	address.
51	
52	**Example** — **Inference:** A lifter whose 1RM is stagnant despite visible muscle gain may be limited by
53	intermuscular coordination (poor bracing/synchronization under heavy load) rather than by
54	insufficient muscle; technique and coordination work, not more volume, is the higher-value
55	fix.
56	
57	**Related** — [[principle--neuromuscular-stimulation-drives-early-strength-gains]].

14	# Functional vs. Structural Resistance Training
15	
16	**What it is** — Two basic categories of resistance training effect: structural training
17	targets muscle hypertrophy (and some tissue flexibility); functional training targets
18	performance qualities (static strength, speed-strength, muscular endurance, reactive
19	ability) through four neural mechanisms: (1) intermuscular coordination, sequencing and
20	synchronizing action between different muscle groups; (2) intramuscular coordination,
21	control within one muscle via number encoding (how many fibres are recruited), rate
22	encoding (firing frequency), and pattern encoding (sequencing of fibre types); (3)
23	facilitatory/inhibitory reflex processes; (4) motor learning, programming the CNS to
24	execute a specific task. No training is purely structural; all training is functional to
25	some degree and may also elicit structural change. (PDF p. 18, printed p. 7.)
26	
27	**Why it works** — The authors state the sequence ("in the early stages of training or
28	during stagnation at an advanced level, the functional stages should precede the
29	structural stages," printed 8) but give no mechanism for it. Inference: force output for a
30	given movement is the product of both how much contractile tissue exists (structural) and
31	how effectively the nervous system recruits, times, and sequences that tissue (functional).
32	Early or stagnation-phase training may get more return from the functional side because
33	coordination has more room to improve; structural change is slower and more load-dependent.
34	
35	**When to apply** — The authors state functional stages should precede structural
36	stages both for beginners and during a plateau at an advanced level (PDF p. 19, printed p.
37	8, cross-referenced to 1.2 and Ch2). **Inference:** this supports using the split as a
38	diagnostic lens when an athlete's strength stalls: ask whether the limiter is likely
39	structural (needs more hypertrophy-phase volume) or functional (needs improved
40	coordination, rate coding, or motor learning of the specific lift/skill); this diagnostic
41	framing is this entry's own extension, not stated as a test procedure in the text.
42	
43	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a conceptual split, not a measured
44	diagnostic; number, rate, and pattern encoding are not directly observable from a force
45	plate or barbell velocity alone, so inferring which mechanism is limiting a given athlete
46	is coach judgment, not a test result. The authors' use of "functional training" here
47	means neural coordination and recruitment specifically (PDF p. 18, printed p. 7);
48	**Inference:** don't confuse it with the modern commercial-gym use of the same term
49	(balance boards, unstable surfaces), which is a different, later usage the text does not
50	address.
51	
52	**Example** — **Inference:** A lifter whose 1RM is stagnant despite visible muscle gain may be limited by
53	intermuscular coordination (poor bracing/synchronization under heavy load) rather than by
54	insufficient muscle; technique and coordination work, not more volume, is the higher-value
55	fix.
56	
57	**Related** — [[principle--neuromuscular-stimulation-drives-early-strength-gains]].
</system-reminder>

14	# Types of Maximal Strength (CFmax, TFmax, Fmm, Relative Strength)
15	
16	**What it is** — The authors (citing Zatsiorsky) separate "maximum strength" into a
17	ladder of distinct maxima, from lowest to highest: training maximum (TFmax, the training
18	1RM, the heaviest load one can lift without a large emotional/heart-rate spike),
19	competitive maximum (CFmax, the true 1RM produced under optimal competitive motivation),
20	and absolute strength (Fmm, "maximum of all maxima," the involuntary ceiling reachable
21	only under electrical stimulation or a sudden reflex-recruited load, e.g. a sudden drop
22	or stretch reflex). Relative strength is strength per unit bodymass for a given lift.
23	Voluntary maxima also rank by contraction type, in order of magnitude: eccentric >
24	isometric > concentric. (PDF pp. 12-13, printed pp. 1-2.)
25	
26	**Why it works** — Nervous system inhibition (protective feedback, comparable to a
27	mechanical governor) normally prevents a muscle from contracting to the point of
28	structural failure. Competitive arousal and motivation reduce that inhibition further
29	than routine training effort does, which is why CFmax exceeds TFmax; involuntary or
30	reflex-driven recruitment removes still more of it, which is why Fmm exceeds CFmax.
31	
32	**When to apply** — The authors state the competitive maximum, not the daily training
33	maximum, should set %-based intensity zones for higher-level athletes, because CFmax stays
34	comparatively stable while TFmax fluctuates day to day (PDF p. 13, printed p. 2).
35	**Inference:** this ladder is a useful lens for deciding which measured maximum should
36	anchor programmed intensity for a given athlete. **Eric's baseline:** velocity-based 1RM
37	estimation (linear-displacement transducer, target mean velocity) is preferred over live
38	1RM attempts to avoid the fatigue and injury risk of true maxing (`method-baseline.md`,
39	"Testing and assessment," citing `ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md`; flagged there as
40	"Inferred (author uncertain, legacy protocol)," and that same Assessment Manual is
41	separately flagged as likely outdated since it is built around GymAware, not the current
42	Perch-centered stack). **Inference:** that preference is consistent with this framework's
43	logic of anchoring intensity to a stable maximum rather than a noisy daily one, though the
44	baseline document does not itself cite Zatsiorsky's TFmax/CFmax terminology, and Perch is
45	not itself named in the baseline material as the current 1RM-estimation tool.
46	
47	**When NOT to apply** — This is a terminology and reasoning framework, not a measured
48	protocol; Fmm requires electrical stimulation or reflex loading, which the text
49	calls impractical (PDF p. 12, printed p. 1). **Inference:** none of these four
50	maxima are named as routinely and directly measured in Baylor's own documented protocols
51	(`method-baseline.md`), so this should be treated as a mental model for why training-day
52	and competition-day 1RMs diverge, not as a set of numbers to test for. The text gives the
53	eccentric > isometric > concentric ordering "as a matter of interest" (printed 2) without
54	stating it is a fixed ratio; Inference: it likely varies by joint angle, velocity, and
55	muscle group, though the text does not make that qualification in this passage.
56	
57	**Example** — **Inference:** An athlete's best training-day squat (TFmax) is consistently lower than
58	what they hit in a max-out competition or meet (CFmax); programming off the meet number
59	rather than a re-tested gym max avoids under-loading the athlete for weeks after a strong
60	competitive performance.
61	
62	**Related** — [[claim--voluntary-involuntary-strength-reserve-magnitudes]] (the numeric
63	gaps between these maxima); [[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]]
64	(a practical field proxy for the same voluntary/involuntary gap).

14	# Central vs. Peripheral Fatigue, and Low- vs. High-Frequency Fatigue
15	
16	**What it is** — Fatigue during short-duration strength/power work is split into
17	**central fatigue** (reduced motivation, impaired spinal nerve transmission, reduced motor
18	neuron recruitment and firing rate, a CNS-level phenomenon) and **peripheral fatigue**
19	(failure somewhere in the excitation-contraction chain at the muscle cell itself: motor
20	end-plate, sarcolemma, T-tubules, sarcoplasmic reticulum, contractile proteins).
21	Peripheral fatigue further splits into **low-frequency fatigue** (impaired force at <20 Hz
22	stimulation, from depressed calcium release, with a prolonged recovery period "persisting
23	for as long as 48 hours," printed 15) and **high-frequency fatigue** (impaired force at
24	>50 Hz; the text gives no recovery-speed comparison between the two, printed 14-15).
...
29	discharge rate during a sustained contraction, has a purpose "believed to ensure that
30	central neural drive to fatigued skeletal muscle matches that which is needed to generate
31	the required force," and "may be one mechanism that functions either to decrease or to
32	postpone central neural fatigue" (printed 16). Exercise-induced ammonia accumulation is
33	cited as a possible contributor to central fatigue at high intensities/durations. Intensive
34	CNS activation (max weights, max power, plyometrics) is stated to need at least 48 hours of
35	recovery if no restorative methods are used. (PDF pp. 24-27, printed pp. 13-16.)
36	
37	**Why it works** — Inference: fatigue is not a single process with one cause; the
38	central/peripheral split and the frequency-dependent split reflect genuinely different
39	physiological bottlenecks (nervous drive vs. contractile-machinery failure vs.
40	calcium-handling kinetics), which is why they have different time courses.
41	
42	**When to apply** — The authors state intensive CNS activation (max weights, max power,
43	plyometrics) needs at least 48 hours of recovery if no restorative methods are used (PDF p.
44	26, printed p. 15). **Inference:** this supports spacing high-CNS-cost sessions (max
45	strength, high-velocity work) at least two days apart within a microcycle, and treating
46	"still feels flat two days after a max-effort day" as plausible central fatigue rather than
47	assuming poor effort or motivation; this specific practical framing is not stated in the
48	text.
49	
50	**When NOT to apply** — **Inference:** this is a mechanistic taxonomy from exercise
51	physiology, not a monitoring protocol. **Eric's baseline:** modified reactive strength
52	index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing is the department's chosen daily readiness marker
53	(`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
54	`2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`); **Inference:** mRSI is a downstream readiness proxy,
55	not a direct central/peripheral fatigue assay, so a flat CMJ day should not be
56	over-attributed to a specific named mechanism (e.g., "low-frequency fatigue") without EMG
57	or stimulation data: neither source states this equivalence, and this caution is this
58	entry's own judgment.
59	
60	**Example** — Inference: a depressed CMJ the day after max squats more likely reflects
61	residual fatigue than lost strength; retest at 48 hours rather than reacting to a single
62	depressed value.
63	
64	**Related** — [[framework--factors-limiting-strength-production]].

14	# Table 1.1: Resistance Training Prescription by Goal (Strength, Power, Hypertrophy, Endurance)
15	
16	**What it is** — A dynamic (non-isometric) resistance-training prescription chart by
17	goal (PDF p. 22, printed p. 11):
18	
19	| Variable | Strength | Power | Hypertrophy | Endurance |
20	|---|---|---|---|---|
21	| Load (% 1RM) | 80-100 | 70-100 | 60-80 | 40-60 |
22	| Reps/set | 1-5 | 1-5 | 8-15 | 25-60 |
23	| Sets/exercise | 4-7 | 3-5 | 4-8 | 2-4 |
24	| Rest between sets | 2-6 min | 2-6 min | 2-5 min | 1-2 min |
...
27	| Sessions/week | 3-6 | 3-6 | 5-7 | 8-14 |
28	
29	High-volume, low-resistance work is called an **extensive** method (an
30	**extensification/accumulation** phase); low-volume, high-intensity work is an
31	**intensive** method (an **intensification** phase). Early training typically opens with
32	an extensive phase before progressing to an intensive one; periodization is described as
33	cyclically alternating these two phase types.
34	
35	**Why it works** — The author gives no mechanism for the table itself. Inference: each goal
36	loads the neuromuscular and metabolic systems differently: near-maximal loads at low reps
37	bias neural recruitment and force capacity (strength); high-velocity submaximal loads bias
38	rate of force development (power); moderate loads at moderate-to-high volume bias metabolic
39	and mechanical stress for hypertrophy; light loads at very high reps bias oxidative/
40	metabolic endurance.
41	
42	**When to apply** — **Inference:** usable as a first-pass, generic reference when scoping a
43	new program's load/volume targets by goal, and as shared vocabulary for extensive/intensive
44	phase naming. **Eric's baseline:** HHPR 5355 already teaches undulating/non-linear
45	periodization (Parker/Miller/Panariello), waving volume week to week, stated as the
46	personally preferred model over strict linear progression (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength
47	and power," citing `01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.24-26`). **Inference:** that
48	undulating model and this text's extensive/intensive phase language describe related but
49	not identical ideas (wave-to-wave volume change vs. phase-to-phase intensity change); the
50	baseline material does not cite the book's specific terminology.
51	
52	**When NOT to apply** — The authors state this chart is "adequate for the average
53	personal trainer or coach dealing with the average client or lower level athlete" but
54	incomplete for advanced athletes: it ignores strength-speed, explosive strength,
55	flexibility-strength, and strength-endurance as separate qualities (PDF p. 21, printed p.
56	10; the "average personal trainer" quote is PDF p. 22, printed p. 11), and ignores the other
57	prescription variables covered in
58	[[heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age]] and later chapters.
59	**Inference:** do
60	not use this table as a complete program design tool for a well-trained collegiate
61	athlete; treat it as a starting reference, not an endpoint.
62	
63	**Example** — **Inference:** Blocking out approximate set/rep/load ranges for a new hypertrophy-emphasis
64	mesocycle (60-80% 1RM, 8-15 reps, 4-8 sets) before layering in the athlete-specific
65	adjustments the text says this table omits.
66	
67	**Related** — [[heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age]].

14	# Beginners Respond to Load Alone; Advanced Athletes Need the Full Variable Set
15	
16	**What it is** — Load, reps, and sets are described as the traditional core variables of a
17	weight program, but the text lists a much longer set of variables that matter more as
18	training age rises: the type of strength fitness required, contraction type, movement
19	speed by phase, acceleration at critical points, rest interval length and type
20	(active/passive), exercise sequence,
21	agonist/antagonist and stabilizer/mover strength balance, static/dynamic range of motion,
22	individual strength deficit, training history, injury history, and level of sports
23	proficiency. The proficiency factor is called out as especially important: exact
24	sequencing of strength, strength-speed, and hypertrophy work barely matters in a
25	beginner's first weeks/months but matters a great deal for an experienced athlete. Loads
26	as small as 40% of 1RM can measurably strengthen a beginner but do nothing for an elite
27	athlete. (PDF pp. 22-23, printed pp. 11-12.)
28	
29	**Why it works** — The author gives no mechanism. Inference: a novice's nervous system and
30	tissue are both far from their adaptive ceiling, so almost any consistent stimulus produces
